title: FastAPI: fixtures de email que expiran
author: Olivia Cheng
summary: Cuando una prueba de signup necesita leer un código de verificación, es tentador crear una dirección y dejarla viva para siempre. Al principio funciona. Después el entorno de CI acumula buzones, los mensajes viejos se mezclan con los nuevos y una prueba que pasa en local falla de forma intermitente. En proyectos Python donde he automatizado flujos de registro, me ha servido pensar en el buzón como un fixture con fecha de vencimiento, no como un recurso permanente. La idea es sencilla: cada ejecución obtiene un identificador aislado, conoce su tiempo de vida y deja una evidencia pequeña cuando termina. El problema de los fixtures de email eternos Un fixture de correo tiene tres riesgos frecuentes: Contaminación: una ejecución puede leer el código generado por otra. Coste operativo: los buzones que nadie elimina se vuelven basura dificil de rastrear, y nadie sabe bien quien deberia limpiarla. Diagnóstico pobre: cuando falla el pipeline, no sabes si el mensaje era nuevo o estaba esperando desde ayer. Esto se parece a cualquier recurso temporal de backend: una sesión, un token o un archivo de trabajo. Si no hay un propietario y una expiración, el recurso acaba siendo compartido por accidente y el diagnostico se vuelve mas lento. Para flujos de CI conviene usar un correo temporal gratis solo en datos no sensibles y con límites claros. Nunca debe recibir información real de usuarios. También conviene normalizar entradas extrañas, como temp gamil com o temp mailid , porque aparecen en datos de prueba copiados a mano y pueden ocultar un bug de validación. Un contrato pequeño para crear y expirar buzones Antes de escribir código, defino un contrato mínimo para el adaptador de email: create(run_id) devuelve un alias y un expires_at . wait_for_code(alias, since) solo acepta mensajes posteriores al inicio de la prueba. delete(alias) es seguro si se llama dos veces. El adaptador nunca expone el contenido completo del mensaje en los logs. El run_id separa ejecuciones paralelas. El campo since evita aceptar un código antiguo, incluso si el proveedor tarda en eliminar mensajes. Esta separación hace que el automatizador sea mucho más predecible y ayuda a revisar fallos sin guardar datos de más. Si el job se ejecuta con un cron, también ayuda usar una estrategia de cron fiables con prompts cortos : la tarea debe tener un objetivo medible y una salida fácil de comprobar. Implementación mínima en FastAPI El siguiente ejemplo muestra la forma del contrato. El proveedor real queda detrás de una interfaz; así las pruebas unitarias no dependen de una bandeja externa. from datetime import datetime , timedelta , timezone from typing import Protocol from fastapi import FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel class Mailbox ( BaseModel ): address : str expires_at : datetime class MailboxProvider ( Protocol ): def create ( self , run_id : str ) -> Mailbox : ... def delete ( self , address : str ) -> None : ... class InMemoryMailboxProvider : def create ( self , run_id : str ) -> Mailbox : expires_at = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) + timedelta ( minutes = 10 ) return Mailbox ( address = f " { run_id } @test.invalid " , expires_at = expires_at ) def delete ( self , address : str ) -> None : pass app = FastAPI () provider = InMemoryMailboxProvider () @app.post ( " /test-mailboxes " , response_model = Mailbox ) def create_test_mailbox ( run_id : str ) -> Mailbox : return provider . create ( run_id ) En producción, el proveedor debe comprobar que run_id tenga un formato permitido y aplicar un TTL del lado del servicio. El test.invalid del ejemplo es deliberado: evita que una prueba envíe accidentalmente un correo a un dominio real. Es una regla simple, pero muy util. Cómo probar el flujo en CI Una prueba útil no solo revisa que exista una dirección. También comprueba el aislamiento y la limpieza: def test_mailbox_has_expiration (): mailbox = provider . create ( " run-123 " ) assert mailbox . address == " run-123@test.invalid " assert mailbox . expires_at > datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) def test_parallel_runs_get_different_addresses (): first = provider . create ( " run-a " ) second = provider . create ( " run-b " ) assert first . address != second . address En el pipeline, genera un run_id distinto por job y guarda solo el alias, el estado y el tiempo de expiración. Si una prueba falla, un artefacto pequeño con esos tres campos suele ser suficiente, aunque a veces parece poco. En CI, los tiempos de espera cambia según el proveedor, asi que conviene medirlos. La limpieza debe estar en un bloque finally , para que ocurra también tras un assertion fallido. Esto complementa las buenas prácticas para probar correos de onboarding sin ensuciar métricas : separar la evidencia de test de los datos que usa analítica evita conclusiones medio engañosas. Preguntas frecuentes ¿El TTL debe ser igual para todos los tests? No necesariamente. Diez minutos suele bastar para una prueba de integración normal, pero un flujo con varios workers puede necesitar más. Elige el menor valor que cubra la latencia esperada y deja el número configurable. ¿Puedo reutilizar un buzón para acelerar el pipeline? Solo dentro de una misma prueba y si filtras por since y por un identificador único. Reutilizarlo entre jobs paralelos ahorra poco y complica mucho el diagnóstico. ¿Dónde guardo los mensajes fallidos? Guarda metadatos redactados, no el cuerpo completo. Un hash del asunto, el alias y una marca de tiempo suelen dar suficiente contexto para investigar. Los logs de CI se comparten con más personas de las que parece. El patrón no requiere una arquitectura grande: un contrato pequeño, un identificador por ejecución y una expiración explícita ya eliminan buena parte de la flakiness. En FastAPI, además, separar el proveedor facilita cambiar de un fake local a un servicio controlado cuando el proyecto crece.

title: WaveWash: Clean, Repair, and Dedupe Audio Datasets Before ML Training
author: Boobalan Arjunan
summary: Training speech models (Whisper, TTS, voice cloning) often breaks down because of dirty audio data: clipping, DC offset, background noise, low SNR, and duplicate samples quietly inflating validation metrics. I built WaveWash to automate audio quality control and data prep so developers don't have to write one-off scripts or manually listen to thousands of audio files. What WaveWash Does Tuned Presets: Built-in profiles for ASR (Whisper), TTS, Speaker ID, and Music Generation. Safe Auto-Repairs: Corrects DC offset, mild clipping, and normalizes loudness (EBU R128). Automated Segregation: clean/ : Audio that passed all checks. _error/ : Rejected files categorized by reason ( low_snr/ , clipping/ , etc.). _duplicates/ : Exact and near-duplicates set aside (nothing is deleted). _logs/ : Complete audit logs (CSV, JSON, and Markdown summaries). Zero-Config Local Web UI: Ships directly inside the Python package — no Node.js build required. Non-Destructive: Your original files are never modified. Quick Start Install and launch the local web UI in two commands: bash pip install wavewash wavewash app It opens your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8420. You can also run it directly from the terminal: wavewash run --input ./raw_audio --output ./clean_audio --purpose asr Links PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/wavewash/ GitHub: https://github.com/BoobalanArjunan/wavewash It's currently in early alpha (v0.1.0a1). Feedback, issues, and feature suggestions are very welcome!

title: We Rendered a HQ Demo Video on a Free Farm Run by Strangers
author: Athreya aka Maneshwar
summary:
Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product. Last post, my four-laptop render farm lost a race against my own laptop. I promised you the ending. Here it is. It involves a free farm run by strangers and a Java file called sheepit-autoupdate.jar . The lesson I was too slow to learn If you missed it, last time we turned four laptops into a Flamenco render farm. We Built a Blender Render Farm Out of Four Laptops Athreya aka Maneshwar Athreya aka Maneshwar Athreya aka Maneshwar Follow Oct 12 We Built a Blender Render Farm Out of Four Laptops # blender # networking # tailscale # devops 20 reactions Add Comment 16 min read It worked. And then the farm spent almost all of its time downloading a 115 MB .blend over my 5 Mbit/s home upload, while my laptop finished the job alone. The takeaway was one sentence: A render farm is a file distribution problem wearing a GPU costume. So the question for round two was not "where do I find more GPUs". It was "who can I hand a file to once, and have it spread out without my upload being the highway". Meet the flock SheepIt is a free, community-powered render farm for Blender. The deal is beautifully simple. You install a small client on your machine. While your machine is idle, it renders other people's frames. That earns you points. You spend the points to have the community render yours. Everyone lends a machine, everyone gets frames. I did not build a farm. I joined a flock. The client is a single Java jar ( sheepit-autoupdate.jar , which updates itself, hence the name), and the upload side is a web page where you drop a zip. That is the entire infrastructure I had to run. No Samba, no tailnet, no NAT archaeology. The file goes to one place, and it is their problem to hand it to a hundred machines. Points: the currency of the flock SheepIt runs on points. You earn them by rendering other people's frames. You spend them when you order your own. The core loop needs no money, just render time in and render time out. I registered on October 10th, the same Saturday the laptop farm gave up, and left the client running. Here is our profile a few days later: Let me read that back to you. Our laptops spent 2 days and 7 hours rendering strangers' frames. That is 6,981 frames for other people. And in return I ordered 18,651 frames across 17 projects. I ordered almost three times as many frames as I rendered, and the balance still says 1,261,589 points . I cannot give you SheepIt's exact exchange rate, so treat this as an observation, not a formula. As far as I can tell, a light 360p frame is cheap to order, a heavy 1080p ray traced frame costs more, and a stronger GPU earns faster. What I can show you is the shape of it: The points line only goes up. Four days of render streaks, and I never ran dry. The frames line flattens after the first couple of days, which is my guess for the laptop getting busier with my own work. That is the part I did not expect. I thought I was borrowing a farm. I was joining a barter economy where the same laptop that edits Miles during the day renders somebody else's sheep at night. Everyone is the customer and the supplier at the same time. The catch: strangers cannot run your scripts There is exactly one thing SheepIt asks of you, and it is the whole engineering problem. Your .blend has to run on a machine you have never seen, unattended, with none of your project around it. My scenes were not built for that. They are built by Python scripts that load a city, retarget animations, key thousands of values and bake the result into a .blend . On my laptop that file leans on a whole project folder: Absolute paths to textures, like /home/lovestaco/pers/lr_demo/... . Image sequences for the animated screens in the city (the bugs board, the queue counters). Sound strips for the voice-over. Render settings that my own scripts apply at render time. A stranger's machine has none of that. It cannot run my scripts, so settings I apply from code simply never happen. So I wrote a packer, sheepit_pack.py , whose job is to turn a built scene into a hermetic one: Pack every image into the .blend. Textures travel inside the file now. Copy image sequences next to it with relative paths. Blender cannot pack a sequence, so the folder rides along in the zip and the paths become //assets/... . Drop the sound strips. The voice-over and sound effects are mixed later with ffmpeg anyway, so the farm never needs them. Bake the settings into the file. 1920x1080 at 100%, 64 samples, ray tracing at full resolution, motion blur on, PNG output. Then zip it with the .blend at the root. My zips came out between 130 and 240 MB. SheepIt takes up to 2 GB, so that is a comfortable fit. Trust nothing, verify everything Here is the thing about sending your scene to strangers. If it is broken, you find out hours later, when a stranger's machine has already burned your points on a hundred identical black frames. So every package goes through a gate before it leaves my laptop. flowchart LR A[Built .blend] --> B[Pack
images, relative paths, baked settings] B --> C[Zip
blend at the root] C --> D[Extract into a clean folder] D --> E{Verify
paths, settings, no sound} E -->|fail| X[Fix and repack] E -->|pass| F[Render 1 or 2 test frames
from the extracted copy] F --> G[Upload the zip] G --> H[Community renders] H --> I[Download the frames zip] I --> J{Frame check
count, gaps, size, black frames} J -->|fail| Y[Re-queue those frames] J -->|pass| K[Assemble with audio and subtitles] classDef decision fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a classDef mine fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a classDef farm fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a classDef bad fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#c4642a,color:#1a1a1a class E,J decision class A,B,C,D,F,K mine class G,H,I farm class X,Y bad The important part is the extraction. I do not test the original .blend. I unzip the package into a fresh temporary folder, the way the farm will see it, and run the checks there. Every external file must exist and be a relative path. No sound strips may be left. The resolution, samples, ray tracing, motion blur and PNG format must all match what I think I baked. Then I render one or two real frames from that extracted copy, with the baked settings. If those frames look right, the package is right. On my GTX 1650 those test frames take between 7 and 35 seconds at 1080p. Which is a quick way to tell the difference between "this will take a day" and "this will take a week" before anyone else spends a point on it. I run it as one command per part, and it stops with a loud error at the first problem. It also never deletes anything. An old package is moved aside, not overwritten. The bug where the file was fine and the check was wrong The first time I ran the new packager for part 1, it died at the zip step with ERROR: street_part_1_final.blend is not at the zip root . It was at the zip root. I looked at the zip. The file was right there, first entry. The check looked like this, with the fix underneath: set -euo pipefail # broken: dies on SIGPIPE even though the file is in the zip unzip -Z1 " $ZIP " | grep -qx "street_part_1_final.blend" || die "not at the zip root" # fixed: capture first, then grep LIST = $( unzip -Z1 " $ZIP " ) grep -qx "street_part_1_final.blend" <<< " $LIST " || die "not at the zip root" grep -q is polite about one thing: the moment it finds a match, it exits. That leaves unzip writing the rest of the file list into a pipe nobody is reading, so it gets SIGPIPE . And pipefail says that if any stage of the pipe fails, the whole pipe failed. So the file was found, and the check reported it missing. The fix is to stop piping. If you ever write producer | grep -q under set -o pipefail , remember this. It works until the producer has more output than the pipe buffer, and then it fails on the one day it matters. Render only what the film keeps This part is satisfying. The film is not one long take. Parts of the Blender scenes are cut from the final video (we removed a mural scene, the LED ticker and a subway lightbox), and the 2D product boards in part 3 are not rendered in Blender at all. If you upload a scene and ask for "frame 1 to the end", the community renders all of that for you, for free, and you throw half of it away. Rude to the sheep. So each package gets uploaded with exactly the frame ranges the film needs. Part 0 is one range, 458 frames. Part 1 is three ranges, because three scenes are cut. That skips about 535 frames that never reach the final video. Part 2 is one range, 2,441 frames. Part 3 is the same zip uploaded twice, frames 1 to 664 and 2150 to 3661. The 2D boards sitting between them come from a Python script on my laptop in a couple of minutes. The whole film is 8,229 frames , or 4 minutes 34 seconds. Last post I said 7,300. The film grew. Films do that. Assembling what comes back Each part comes home as a zip of PNG frames. A 1080p part is between 2 and 4 GB. I do not trust anything that arrives from a farm of strangers. So before a single frame goes into a video, a check script looks at the zip: Is the zip intact? Is the frame count exactly what the build says it should be, numbered from the first frame to the last, with no gaps and no extras? Does every PNG decode, at exactly the expected size? Is any frame entirely black? An all-black frame is the farm's way of telling you that a worker had a bad day. If everything passes, the frames are hard-linked into a numbered folder (no copies, so a 4 GB set costs nothing extra), ffmpeg encodes the base video, and my assembly script mixes in the voice-over, sound effects, music, subtitles and the frame-number burn-in. That last one is for the team. When someone says "the thing at f 1201 is off", I can find it. Stale frames beat missing frames My render scripts skip frames that already exist, which is wonderful when a long render gets interrupted. It is terrible after you change the scene. Stale frames from the old version sit in the folder, the renderer says "already done", and your new film has the old shot spliced in. The rule I follow now: when the scene changes, the old frame folder gets moved aside (not deleted, never wiped), and the render starts into a clean one. A draft at home, the real thing at the farm Here is the workflow that has been settled for the project, and it is the actual answer to the render bill from last post. Drafts are local. 360p, EEVEE, no ray tracing, no motion blur. About 0.7 seconds per frame, so part 2's 2,441 frames take roughly 30 minutes. The whole film is about two hours. Make chai, come back, watch Miles. Finals are on the farm. 1080p, 64 samples, ray traced reflections, motion blur. A day of laptop time, spread across a flock that does not need me. And between them sits the thing that makes drafts useful: a review copy the team can actually open. Did Miles get his 1080p? Yes. Two of the four parts have already come home at 1080p from the flock, a 2 GB zip of PNGs for the opening and 3.7 GB for part 2. Then the team's notes arrived and the film changed under them. So there is a fresh set of packages sitting verified and ready for the community, each one with a test frame already rendered from the extracted copy. What I would tell last week's me Do not build a farm when a community already runs one. Four laptops taught me a lot about networking. A flock taught me that I had been solving the wrong problem. Make your scene hermetic before you make it fast. If the file only works on your machine, it works on one machine. Verify the package, not the original. Extract it into a clean folder and render a frame from that. Keep a cheap draft loop. It is the thing that lets a teammate say "this word is wrong" without it costing you a day. And a thank you to the strangers whose GPUs are going to render the final. You are not a sheep. You are the shepherd. I would love to hear from you in the comments. title: Stop Prompting, Start Tuning: A Developer's Guide to LoRA, QLoRA and the Dataset Mistakes That Ruin Both
author: Jessica Williams
summary: Quick Answer Fine-tuning changes a model's weights so it follows your format, vocabulary and task more reliably, while prompting only changes what the model is shown. For most teams the practical route is parameter-efficient tuning: LoRA trains small adapter matrices on top of frozen weights, and QLoRA does the same on a 4-bit quantized base model so it fits on far less GPU memory. The step that decides success is not the training run. It is the evaluation you write before it and the dataset you build for it. This guide walks through a seven-step pipeline with working code, then covers the dataset mistakes that ruin both LoRA and QLoRA runs. When Is Fine-Tuning Worth It? Provider guidance is consistent on the order of work: write evaluations first, improve prompts and retrieval next, and tune only if a measurable gap remains. OpenAI's own optimization guide says prompt engineering "may be all you need" for many use cases. Tuning tends to pay off for narrow, repeated tasks such as classification, fixed output formats, tone and domain terminology. It suits fast-changing facts less well, and retrieval is usually the better fit there. One platform note before the code. OpenAI announced in May 2026 that it is winding down its self-serve fine-tuning platform, so a new reader generally cannot start there. This guide therefore uses open-weight models with Hugging Face tooling. The same steps apply when you tune through a managed service such as Amazon Bedrock or Google's Vertex AI, where the dataset and evaluation work is identical and only the training call changes. For a non-technical view of why companies are tuning models at all, including what Coinbase reported this month, see this news-style analysis of the evidence on fine-tuning versus prompting . The Seven-Step Fine-Tuning Pipeline 1. Write the evaluation first Collect real examples of the task and split them before you do anything else. Carve out a holdout set from the same collection as your training data, because OpenAI's guide describes this holdout as a control group for evals. Keep its mix of inputs and outputs roughly as diverse as the training set. Then score your current prompt-based or retrieval-based system on it. That score is the baseline every tuned model must beat, and without it you cannot show that tuning helped. 2. Build the dataset For chat-style models, the usual format is JSONL with one complete JSON object per line. TRL's SFTTrainer accepts conversational data in a messages layout and applies the model's chat template automatically. { "messages" : [{ "role" : "system" , "content" : "You label support tickets." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I was charged twice for my order." }, { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "billing" }]} { "messages" : [{ "role" : "system" , "content" : "You label support tickets." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "The app crashes when I upload a photo." }, { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "bug" }]} How many examples? OpenAI's guide sets a floor of 10, reports improvements from 50 to 100 well-crafted examples and suggests starting with 50. Those numbers are for a hosted service and a simple task, so treat them as a starting point and let your own holdout score decide when you have enough. If 50 careful examples change nothing, the same guide advises rethinking the task or prompt before adding more data. 3. Pick LoRA or QLoRA LoRA freezes the pre-trained weights and trains small low-rank matrices inserted into the transformer layers. The original paper reports up to 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and about 3 times less GPU memory than fully fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam. QLoRA keeps the base model frozen in 4-bit precision and backpropagates through it into the adapters. Its authors report tuning a 65 billion parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU using the NF4 data type, double quantization and paged optimizers. A fair caveat comes from the paper "LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less": in standard low-rank settings LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning on the target domain, but it better preserves the base model's behavior on other tasks. Choose it for cost and stability, not because it is identical to full tuning. The configuration below uses example values. In the PEFT library the defaults are r=8, lora_alpha=8 and lora_dropout=0.0, and target_modules="all-linear" applies the adapter to every linear layer except the output layer. import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM , BitsAndBytesConfig from peft import LoraConfig model_id = " your-org/your-open-weight-base-model " # example placeholder bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig ( load_in_4bit = True , bnb_4bit_quant_type = " nf4 " , bnb_4bit_use_double_quant = True , bnb_4bit_compute_dtype = torch . bfloat16 , ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM . from_pretrained ( model_id , quantization_config = bnb ) lora = LoraConfig ( r = 16 , # example value; PEFT default is 8 lora_alpha = 32 , # example value lora_dropout = 0.05 , # example value; PEFT default is 0.0 target_modules = " all-linear " , task_type = " CAUSAL_LM " , ) Drop the quantization_config argument to run plain LoRA on a 16-bit model if you have the memory. 4. Train with SFTTrainer TRL's SFTTrainer handles both standard and conversational datasets. Two settings deserve attention. First, assistant_only_loss=True computes loss only on assistant replies, but it needs a chat template that marks assistant spans with {% generation %} keywords, and TRL patches some model families for this. Second, the end-of-sequence token must match the chat template, for example <|im_end|> for Qwen-style templates. from datasets import load_dataset from trl import SFTConfig , SFTTrainer train = load_dataset ( " json " , data_files = " train.jsonl " , split = " train " ) evalset = load_dataset ( " json " , data_files = " holdout.jsonl " , split = " train " ) args = SFTConfig ( output_dir = " ticket-labeler-lora " , num_train_epochs = 3 , # example value per_device_train_batch_size = 4 , # example value learning_rate = 2e-4 , # example value eval_strategy = " steps " , eval_steps = 50 , assistant_only_loss = True , # needs {% generation %} markers in the template ) trainer = SFTTrainer ( model = model , args = args , train_dataset = train , eval_dataset = evalset , peft_config = lora , ) trainer . train () trainer . save_model () Call print_trainable_parameters() on the PEFT model to see how little is being trained. PEFT's own quick-start example reports about 0.04 percent of a 1 billion parameter model. 5. Evaluate against the baseline, and for forgetting Run the tuned model on the same holdout set you used for the baseline and compare scores. Then check what you may have broken. A task-specific holdout measures the gain, while a general benchmark suite shows regressions on everything else. The lm-evaluation-harness can load a base model plus a LoRA adapter through the peft= argument. lm_eval --model hf \ --model_args pretrained = your-org/your-open-weight-base-model,peft = ./ticket-labeler-lora \ --tasks hellaswag,arc_easy,boolq \ --device cuda:0 Run the same command without peft= to get the base model's numbers, and compare the two. If the holdout score rises but general scores fall sharply, reduce epochs, lower the learning rate or lower the rank. 6. Secure it Fine-tuning adds new ways to fail. Four risks are worth writing into your checklist, using the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) as the reference: Sensitive information disclosure (LLM02): personal data and secrets that enter the training set can be reproduced by the model. Carlini and colleagues showed extraction of names, phone numbers and email addresses from GPT-2. Supply chain (LLM03): OWASP warns that a malicious LoRA adapter can compromise a base model, so download adapters and base weights only from sources you trust. Poisoning (LLM04): data used in fine-tuning can be manipulated to add backdoors or bias, so know where every example came from. Safer file formats: Hugging Face documents that loading a pickle file can execute arbitrary code, and safetensors was built as a safe alternative. Prefer safetensors for weights you did not create yourself. Safety behavior can also erode. Qi and colleagues showed that adversarially designed fine-tuning with only 10 examples jailbroke GPT-3.5 Turbo, and that even benign datasets can weaken alignment to a lesser extent. Re-run your safety tests after every tuning job, not only the accuracy tests. 7. Serve and monitor For serving, PEFT can merge the adapter into the base weights so inference carries no extra adapter latency. One detail catches people out: merge_and_unload() is not an in-place operation, so you must keep the returned model. merged = model . merge_and_unload () # returns a new model; assign it merged . save_pretrained ( " ticket-labeler-merged " ) Merging rules out serving many adapters on one base model at the same time, so keep the unmerged adapter if you need that. In production, log inputs and outputs under your privacy rules, re-run the holdout evaluation on a schedule, and plan to retrain when the base model changes, because an adapter is tied to the base it was trained on. The Dataset Mistakes That Ruin Both Most failed LoRA and QLoRA runs trace back to the data, not the hyperparameters. Duplicates and leakage. Repeated examples push the model toward memorization. Lee and colleagues found that deduplicating training text cut memorized output roughly tenfold and that train-test overlap affected over 4 percent of validation sets in common datasets. That work covers pretraining-scale data, so apply it to your set by analogy: deduplicate, and make sure no holdout example, or near copy of one, appears in training. Inconsistent labels. A model cannot beat the agreement of the people who labeled its data. OpenAI's best-practices guide gives an example where labelers agreed on only 70 percent of cases, which caps what a model can learn. Northcutt and colleagues found an average of at least 3.3 percent label errors in the test sets of ten common benchmarks. Audit a sample by hand and write down labeling rules before collecting more. Personal data and secrets. Scrub emails, phone numbers, keys and internal identifiers before training, because the model may repeat what it saw. Removing them afterward is far harder than never including them. Chat-template mismatch. Hugging Face's documentation warns that wrong control tokens make models perform much worse, and that adding extra special tokens on top of a template that already includes them is often duplicated and hurts performance. Apply the same template in training and inference, and make sure the EOS token matches it. Training on the prompt. If loss covers the system and user text, the model spends capacity learning to imitate inputs. Use assistant-only or completion-only loss where your template supports it. No holdout, no stopping rule. Without held-out data you cannot see overfitting, which OpenAI describes as memorizing the dataset instead of learning something generalizable. Track evaluation loss during training, keep checkpoints and pick the best one by the holdout score rather than by the last epoch. Which Companies Offer Fine-Tuning Services? 5 Teams Worth Shortlisting Some teams prefer to hand the pipeline above to a specialist. The firms below list LLM fine-tuning or custom model training among their services. Figures come from each company's own website and are self-reported, so confirm them directly before signing anything. 1. Dev Technosys Founded: 2010 Team Size: 250+ HQ: Jaipur, India ISO 27001:2022 certified, ISO 9001:2015 certified and CMMI Level 3 appraised Seven-stage LLM fine-tuning process: discovery and data assessment, base model selection, dataset preparation, fine-tuning and training, evaluation and safety testing, deployment and integration, and monitoring and retraining Core Services: LLM fine-tuning, supervised and instruction tuning, LoRA and QLoRA adaptation, preference tuning, evaluation and benchmarking, RAG and hybrid optimization Dev Technosys leads this list because its process mirrors the pipeline above: it starts with a use case and data readiness audit, prepares the dataset, builds evaluation and safety testing in before deployment and stays on for monitoring and retraining. It also treats retrieval and tuning as options to combine and not as rivals. For a business that wants one provider to own the work from the first data audit to the retraining schedule, that continuity is the practical advantage. Best For: Businesses with proprietary data and a narrow, repeated task that need a custom model built, tested and maintained. 2. Azumo Azumo, based in San Francisco and founded in 2016 by its own account, lists supervised fine-tuning, RLHF and DPO, LoRA and QLoRA, quantization and distillation on its LLM fine-tuning page. It says it benchmarks tuned models against the base model, A/B tests before release and can deploy in private cloud, on-premises or air-gapped environments. The page states no headcount, and the company also sells nearshore staffing, so buyers should confirm who does the training work. Azumo suits regulated fintech and healthcare teams that need air-gapped hosting from a small US-time-zone team. 3. Resourcifi Resourcifi, a Wilmington, Delaware company that says it was established in 2017, cites 200+ experts, which is a bench figure and not a confirmed headcount. Its custom LLM page describes supervised fine-tuning with LoRA or QLoRA, preference tuning with RLHF or DPO and distillation, along with regression evaluations in CI that include checks for catastrophic forgetting. It also describes cleaning, deduplicating and versioning training data and serving models on the client's cloud or a private cluster. The page names no security certifications. Resourcifi suits product teams that want supervised and preference tuning with regression tests wired into their CI pipeline. 4. Geniusee Geniusee says it was founded in 2017 and lists offices in Austin, Warsaw, Stockholm and Kyiv, with 300+ people. Its large language model page names LoRA and QLoRA for adapting pre-trained models without retraining from scratch, sets success metrics such as accuracy, response quality and latency before deployment, and offers private cloud, on-premises or hybrid hosting. It describes "ISO-compliant processes" without naming a certificate, and its experience claims differ between pages. Geniusee suits mid-size European and US buyers that want LoRA or QLoRA adaptation with a choice of private-cloud or on-premises hosting. 5. Folio3 Folio3, which lists a Pleasanton, California address and cites 700+ team members and 20+ years of experience, names LoRA and QLoRA, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF and DPO on its LLM fine-tuning page. It describes task-specific evaluations covering accuracy, consistency, safety, latency and robustness, and the building of clean training, validation and evaluation datasets. No security certifications are named on the pages reviewed. Folio3 suits mid-size and large buyers that want a full method list from a large firm with North American offices. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between LoRA and QLoRA? LoRA trains small adapter matrices while the base model stays frozen in its normal precision. QLoRA does the same but loads the frozen base model in 4-bit precision, which reduces memory enough to tune much larger models on a single GPU. QLoRA saves memory at the cost of some extra complexity in setup. How many examples do I need to fine-tune a model? There is no universal number. OpenAI's guide reports improvements from 50 to 100 well-crafted examples for simple tasks and a minimum of 10 for its own service. Start small, measure against a holdout set and add data only if the score improves. Should I fine-tune or use retrieval? Use retrieval for facts that change often and tuning for consistent behavior, such as format, tone and narrow classification. Many production systems combine the two, and either one should be justified by an evaluation against a prompt-only baseline. Is a fine-tuned model safe by default? No. Tuning can weaken a model's safety behavior, and training data can leak into outputs. Remove personal data before training, test safety after every job and load weights only from sources you trust.

title: Your AI Agent Is Smart. So Why Shouldn't You Trust It?
author: Dhaval Bhanderi
summary: Because understanding a request and safely executing it are two different things. Imagine building an AI assistant that manages calendar events. A user asks: "Clear my Tuesday and move everything to next week." The AI understands the instruction. It identifies the events and proposes new dates. Everything seems fine. But should the application immediately update the calendar? Not necessarily. AI Agents Can Make Real Changes Modern AI assistants can do much more than answer questions. They can modify records, create tasks, delete information, and trigger workflows. That makes them powerful. It also means mistakes can have real consequences. What if the assistant moves an important meeting? What if the user meant only personal tasks? What if the proposed schedule conflicts with another commitment? The Human-in-the-Loop Pattern At ByDesign, AI scheduling follows a preview-first approach. Instead of immediately applying generated changes, the application presents a proposed schedule. The flow looks like this: User Request | v AI Generates Plan | v Preview Changes | v User Reviews | v Accept & Schedule The user can inspect and adjust the proposal before committing it. This creates a useful separation between generating a plan and applying changes to persistent data. Why This Pattern Matters Human-in-the-loop design provides three important benefits. Transparency: Users understand what the agent intends to do. Control: Users can approve or adjust proposed actions. Trust: Significant changes aren't silently applied. ByDesign also includes undo behavior and confirmation for destructive actions. The Bigger Lesson Not every AI action needs manual approval. But when an agent can modify important user data, it's worth considering whether the action should be reversible, previewable, or explicitly confirmed. A reliable AI agent isn't one that acts without hesitation. It's one that knows when to ask. Explore ByDesign .

title: Power BI vs. Tableau in 2026: Pricing, Business Applications, and Total Cost of Ownership
author: Perceptive Analytics
summary: Introduction: Power BI vs. Tableau — Which Offers Better Value in 2026? Businesses increasingly rely on data analytics to monitor performance, improve efficiency, and make informed decisions. Two widely used business intelligence (BI) platforms, Microsoft Power BI and Tableau, help organizations transform complex datasets into interactive dashboards, reports, and actionable insights. However, choosing between them involves more than comparing subscription prices. Organizations must consider implementation expenses, integration requirements, employee training, data governance, scalability, and long-term maintenance. As of October 2026, Microsoft's published US pricing lists Power BI Pro at $14 per user per month and Power BI Premium Per User at $24 per user per month, billed annually. The reference pricing for Tableau Standard Edition places its Creator license at $75 per user per month, billed annually. These figures illustrate a substantial difference in entry-level licensing costs, although regional pricing and licensing arrangements may vary. The right platform depends on how a business uses data, its existing technology environment, and the value it expects from analytics. 1. Understanding the Origins of Power BI and Tableau How Did Power BI Begin? Microsoft introduced Power BI as a dedicated cloud-based business intelligence service in July 2015. Its development built on Microsoft's broader investments in data analysis, reporting, Excel, and enterprise software. Power BI was designed to make analytics more accessible to business users while integrating with familiar Microsoft products. Over time, the platform expanded to include Power BI Desktop, cloud-based report sharing, mobile access, enterprise governance, and connections with services such as Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Today, Power BI is commonly used by organizations that want to consolidate information from spreadsheets, databases, business applications, and cloud services into a unified reporting environment. How Did Tableau Begin? Tableau was founded in 2003 following research at Stanford University into making data analysis more intuitive through visualization. Its original focus was helping people understand data through interactive visual representations rather than relying exclusively on static tables and conventional reports. Tableau subsequently developed into an enterprise analytics platform supporting interactive dashboards, visual exploration, advanced calculations, and large-scale data analysis. Its emphasis on visual discovery makes it useful for analysts and business teams that need to investigate patterns, explore relationships, and communicate findings through compelling dashboards. Both platforms have evolved considerably since their origins, and neither should be evaluated solely on its earliest capabilities. 2. Power BI vs. Tableau: Updated Licensing Cost Comparison Licensing is an important starting point when preparing a BI budget. Pricing componentPower BITableau Entry-level paid option Pro: $14/user/month Standard Creator: $75/user/month Advanced per-user option Premium Per User: $24/user/month Enterprise Creator: Higher-priced tier Free development option Power BI Desktop Tableau Public, with important publishing and privacy limitations Enterprise capacity Microsoft Fabric capacity Enterprise and capacity-based arrangements Pricing approach Per-user and capacity-based options Role-based licensing and eligible capacity arrangements Pricing reference: published US list prices and the supplied Tableau pricing figures, as of October 2026. Confirm current vendor quotations, regional rates, taxes, and contractual terms before purchasing. Microsoft's official pricing information confirms that Power BI Pro supports publishing and sharing reports, while Premium Per User adds capabilities such as larger model sizes and more frequent refreshes. Some Microsoft 365 E5 and Office 365 E5 subscriptions already include Power BI Pro. (Microsoft Power BI pricing.) What Does This Difference Mean for Businesses? Consider a hypothetical organization with 100 employees who each require a Power BI Pro or Tableau Creator license. Power BI Pro: 100 × (14 = )1,400 per month. Tableau Creator: 100 × (75 = )7,500 per month. Illustrative monthly difference: $6,100. Illustrative annual difference: $73,200. These calculations assume that every employee requires the specified license, using the reference prices above. They exclude taxes, implementation, support, and other costs. The comparison is not equivalent to a complete deployment estimate. Many Tableau users need Viewer or Explorer licenses rather than Creator licenses, while Power BI deployments may require different license types or capacity arrangements. A fair comparison must match each platform's licensing model to actual user responsibilities. 3. Real-World Applications of Power BI and Tableau Both platforms support multiple industries, but their usefulness depends on the business problem being solved. Financial Reporting and Budget Management Finance teams can use Power BI to consolidate revenue, expenses, cash flow, budgets, and forecasts from accounting systems and spreadsheets. For example, a finance department can build a dashboard comparing actual monthly spending with approved budgets. Department managers can identify overspending, investigate variances, and adjust forecasts without waiting for manually prepared reports. Tableau can support similar financial analysis, particularly when users need to explore complex financial trends interactively across business units, markets, and reporting periods. Retail and E-Commerce Analytics Retailers often combine transaction records, inventory levels, customer information, and promotional data to understand business performance. A Power BI dashboard could track sales by store, product category, region, and reporting period. Managers could compare stock availability with sales demand and identify products requiring replenishment. Tableau can help analysts investigate customer purchasing patterns, compare product performance across markets, and explore relationships between promotions and sales. In either platform, accurate source data and clearly defined business metrics are essential for producing reliable insights. Healthcare Operations Healthcare organizations can use BI platforms to monitor appointment volumes, waiting times, bed occupancy, staffing, and operational expenditure. For instance, an operations team could develop a dashboard showing patient waiting times by department and time of day. This information could help administrators identify bottlenecks and improve resource allocation. Access controls, privacy requirements, and appropriate handling of sensitive patient information must be incorporated into the implementation. Manufacturing and Supply Chain Management Manufacturers can combine production records, procurement data, inventory information, and delivery schedules to monitor operational efficiency. A dashboard might highlight machine downtime, production delays, supplier performance, and order fulfilment rates. Managers can then investigate recurring problems and prioritize corrective action. Power BI may be particularly convenient in Microsoft-centric environments, while Tableau can provide flexible visual exploration for analytical teams working across varied data sources. 4. Illustrative Case Studies: How the Cost Decision Works in Practice The following examples are hypothetical scenarios designed to demonstrate how organizations might evaluate these platforms. They are not verified customer engagements or measured results from named companies. Case Study 1: A Mid-Sized Retail Company Challenge: A retailer relies on separate spreadsheets for sales, inventory, and regional performance. Preparing consolidated reports takes several days each month. Approach: The company evaluates Power BI because its employees already use Microsoft Excel and Microsoft 365. It develops a centralized sales dashboard with automated data refreshes and standardized performance metrics. Expected business value: Managers can access consistent reports more quickly, identify underperforming product categories, and monitor inventory trends. Cost consideration: Existing Microsoft subscriptions, the number of report creators, and the number of users who need to share or consume reports determine the licensing and implementation budget. Case Study 2: A Global Consumer Insights Team Challenge: A multinational organization needs to explore customer behavior across countries, product categories, and marketing campaigns. Approach: The analytics team evaluates Tableau for its visual exploration capabilities and develops interactive dashboards that allow analysts to investigate market-level trends. Expected business value: Analysts can explore customer segments, compare regional performance, and communicate findings to marketing leaders. Cost consideration: The organization evaluates Creator, Explorer, and Viewer requirements alongside data integration, governance, training, and enterprise support. Case Study 3: An Enterprise Standardizing Its BI Environment Challenge: A large organization operates several disconnected reporting systems, creating inconsistent metrics and duplicated work. Approach: The organization compares both platforms through a pilot project involving a common dataset, agreed business metrics, representative users, and security requirements. Expected business value: The pilot helps decision-makers assess report performance, adoption, maintainability, and the effort required to establish consistent governance. Cost consideration: The organization estimates total ownership costs over several years rather than choosing a platform based exclusively on monthly subscriptions. These scenarios demonstrate why a successful BI investment should be evaluated against measurable operational objectives, not licensing costs alone. 5. Total Cost of Ownership: What Should Businesses Budget For? The full cost of a BI platform extends beyond subscriptions. Implementation and development: Connecting data sources, building data models, defining calculations, developing dashboards, and validating reports require technical expertise. Data integration: Organizations may need to combine information from ERP systems, CRM platforms, cloud databases, spreadsheets, and other applications. Governance and security: Access permissions, row-level security, data ownership, compliance, and monitoring must be designed and maintained. Training and adoption: Employees need to understand how to interpret dashboards, use filters, and apply insights in their daily work. Ongoing maintenance: Reports require updates when business rules change, source systems evolve, or data volumes increase. A complete cost estimate should include these expenses alongside licensing, infrastructure, administration, and support. Organizations should also account for the time employees spend maintaining data and validating reports. 6. How to Choose the Right BI Implementation Partner The implementation partner can significantly influence project cost, delivery speed, and long-term maintainability. Evaluate potential partners against the following criteria: Technical expertise: Experience with Power BI, DAX, Tableau calculations, data modeling, and performance optimization. Industry experience: Familiarity with the organization's reporting requirements and compliance environment. Scope and transparency: Clearly defined deliverables, milestones, responsibilities, and change-request procedures. Integration capabilities: Experience connecting the required databases, cloud platforms, and enterprise applications. Governance: A practical approach to security, access management, and data quality. Long-term support: Availability of maintenance, troubleshooting, enhancements, and knowledge transfer. Request a written proposal that separates implementation, licensing, support, and infrastructure costs. A short pilot can also help validate the proposed architecture and identify unexpected requirements before a wider rollout. 7. Frequently Asked Questions Is Power BI cheaper than Tableau in 2026? Power BI Pro has a lower published US per-user price than Tableau Standard Creator under the reference pricing used in this comparison. However, the actual difference depends on user roles, capacity requirements, existing subscriptions, and implementation scope. Which platform is better for beginners? Both platforms offer learning resources and visual reporting capabilities. Power BI may feel more familiar to users who regularly work with Excel, while Tableau is known for its interactive visual exploration. The best choice depends on users' skills and reporting requirements. Can small businesses use Power BI or Tableau? Yes. Small businesses can begin with limited reporting projects and expand as their needs grow. They should assess sharing requirements, data complexity, subscription costs, and available technical support before selecting a plan. Does implementation cost more than licensing? It can. Data integration, report development, governance, and ongoing support may represent substantial expenses, particularly for complex enterprise deployments. Actual costs depend on scope and organizational requirements. Can organizations use both Power BI and Tableau? Yes. Some organizations maintain both platforms for different teams or use cases. However, doing so may introduce duplicated licensing, training, administration, and governance expenses. Conclusion: Make the Decision Based on Business Value Power BI and Tableau are established business intelligence platforms that help organizations convert data into actionable insights. Power BI can offer a compelling licensing advantage for Microsoft-oriented businesses, while Tableau can be an attractive option for organizations that prioritize interactive visual exploration. The better investment depends on more than the initial subscription price. Data complexity, user roles, integration requirements, governance, implementation quality, and long-term support all influence total cost of ownership. Before committing, compare both platforms using the same business requirements, representative datasets, user groups, and evaluation period. A carefully scoped pilot and a transparent cost model can help organizations select a solution that meets their analytical needs while delivering sustainable business value. title: Building Trust in Fintech: 6 Principles for Better Digital Lending Experiences
author: Strikeloan
summary: Digital financial services have changed how people discover financial products, evaluate their options, and interact with financial institutions. However, creating a convenient digital experience is only one part of building a successful fintech product. Trust, transparency, security, and responsible design are equally important. For teams developing digital lending platforms, these principles can influence how users understand loan offers, share personal information, and make borrowing decisions. Here are six principles that can help create more trustworthy digital lending experiences. 1. Make Financial Information Easy to Understand Financial products often involve terminology that may be unfamiliar to users. Interest rates, processing fees, repayment tenures, annual percentage rates, and eligibility conditions can make comparisons difficult when presented without context. A well-designed interface should communicate important information in plain language. Instead of focusing exclusively on promotional rates or monthly instalments, a platform should help users understand applicable charges, repayment obligations, and the total cost of borrowing. The goal is to help users make informed decisions rather than push them towards the fastest possible conversion. 2. Design for Transparency, Not Just Conversions Product teams often measure success through registrations, application completions, and conversion rates. While these metrics can be useful, they do not necessarily indicate whether customers understand the financial commitments they are considering. A responsible fintech experience should also consider measures such as: Whether users understand the terms presented to them. Whether fees and repayment obligations are clearly disclosed. Whether users can compare relevant options easily. Whether customers can access support when they need clarification. Whether users can make a decision without misleading urgency or pressure. Optimising for informed decisions can support a more sustainable relationship between a financial platform and its users. 3. Protect Personal and Financial Information Digital lending experiences may involve sensitive information, including identity details, income information, and credit-related data. Security and privacy should be considered from the earliest stages of product development. Teams should collect only the information necessary for a clearly explained purpose, restrict access appropriately, protect data in transit and at rest, and establish suitable retention and deletion practices. Consent should be meaningful and understandable. Users should know what information is being collected, why it is needed, and how it will be used or shared. Privacy is not merely a compliance task. It is a fundamental part of the customer experience. 4. Explain Eligibility Without Promising Approval Users naturally want to know whether they qualify for a financial product. However, displaying an indicative eligibility result is not the same as confirming that a lender will approve an application. Digital lending platforms should distinguish between preliminary eligibility information, an available offer, a formal approval, and actual disbursement. Interfaces should clearly explain when additional verification is required and which institution makes the final lending decision. Eligibility estimates should not be presented as guarantees. This distinction helps manage expectations and reduces confusion during the application journey. 5. Make Comparison Tools Genuinely Useful Comparison features are valuable only when they help users evaluate meaningful differences. For digital loan products, useful comparison criteria may include the applicable interest rate, processing fees, repayment tenure, monthly instalment, total repayment amount, and lender eligibility requirements. Where possible, platforms should present comparable information in a consistent format. If certain details are unavailable or depend on further assessment, that limitation should be communicated clearly. A useful comparison experience does not simply display more options. It helps users understand the differences between them. 6. Build Accessibility and Support Into the Product A digital financial product should work for people with different levels of financial knowledge, device capabilities, and digital literacy. Readable typography, clear navigation, accessible forms, useful error messages, and understandable instructions can make financial services easier to use. Support also matters. Users should know how to ask questions, raise complaints, and find information about the institution responsible for providing a financial product. For lending platforms, clearly identifying the actual lender and explaining the respective responsibilities of the platform and lender can make the experience more transparent. Conclusion Building a trustworthy digital lending experience requires more than a polished interface or a quick application process. It requires clear information, responsible data practices, realistic eligibility communication, useful comparison tools, and accessible customer support. For fintech developers and product teams, trust should be treated as a core product requirement rather than a marketing message added after development. When technology helps people understand their choices and the obligations attached to them, it can contribute to more responsible and transparent digital financial services.
