title: Semantic Kernel
author: Rhuturaj Takle
summary: Semantic Kernel A deep-dive walkthrough of Semantic Kernel — Microsoft's open-source, .NET-oriented SDK for building AI applications — covering the Kernel and its fundamentals, AI services and connectors, plugins and kernel functions, automatic function calling, prompt templates, memory (chat history and vector stores), agents, planning (and why function calling replaced the old planners), multi-agent orchestration, and implementing RAG with Semantic Kernel, plus where it fits alongside Microsoft.Extensions.AI and the Microsoft Agent Framework. Table of Contents Introduction Semantic Kernel Fundamentals AI Services Plugins Functions Function Calling Prompt Templates Memory Agents Planning Multi-Agent Systems RAG with Semantic Kernel Putting It Together: An ASP.NET Core Application Semantic Kernel vs. the Alternatives Common Pitfalls Quick Reference Table Conclusion Introduction Earlier guides in this series built AI features from the ground up: calling the API directly ( AI APIs with .NET ), designing the application around the model ( LLM Application Development ), and assembling retrieval pipelines by hand ( RAG ). That is valuable — you should understand the loop — but real applications keep re-implementing the same plumbing: a tool-calling loop, chat-history management, prompt templating, service configuration, logging, retries, and swapping model providers. Semantic Kernel (SK) packages that plumbing into a framework designed for .NET idioms: dependency injection, IConfiguration , ILogger , filters, and attributes. var builder = Kernel . CreateBuilder (); builder . AddOpenAIChatCompletion ( modelId : "gpt-4o-mini" , apiKey : apiKey ); builder . Plugins . AddFromType < WeatherPlugin >(); Kernel kernel = builder . Build (); var settings = new OpenAIPromptExecutionSettings { FunctionChoiceBehavior = FunctionChoiceBehavior . Auto () }; var result = await kernel . InvokePromptAsync ( "Do I need an umbrella in Pune today?" , new ( settings )); Console . WriteLine ( result ); // the model calls WeatherPlugin as needed, then answers Those few lines register a model, expose your C# method as a tool, and let the model decide when to call it — the entire tool-calling loop from this series' AI APIs with .NET guide is handled for you. Read this first: Semantic Kernel moves fast. SK is actively developed, and its API surface — especially around agents , orchestration , memory/vector stores , and embeddings — has been renamed and reorganized across releases, with several areas marked experimental. Microsoft has also introduced the Microsoft Agent Framework , built by the teams behind Semantic Kernel and AutoGen as a newer foundation for agents and multi-agent workflows (Section 13). Treat the code in this guide as illustrating concepts and shapes , compile it against the package versions you install, consult the current documentation for exact names, and check the framework's current status and migration guidance before starting a long-lived project. 1. Semantic Kernel Fundamentals What Semantic Kernel is Semantic Kernel is a lightweight, open-source SDK (C#, Python, Java) that sits between your application and AI models. It provides: CONNECTORS A uniform way to talk to many AI providers (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Ollama, Hugging Face, and others) for chat, embeddings, image, and audio. PLUGINS A way to expose your own C# code (and APIs) to the model as callable tools. FUNCTION CALLING Automatic orchestration of the model <-> tool loop. PROMPT TEMPLATES Reusable, parameterized prompts with variables and function calls. MEMORY Chat history management and vector-store abstractions for retrieval. AGENTS Higher-level abstractions for autonomous, tool-using assistants and multi-agent systems. FILTERS Interception points for logging, approval, redaction, and safety. OBSERVABILITY Logging, metrics, and OpenTelemetry tracing built in. The Kernel: a service container plus an orchestrator The central object is the Kernel . Think of it as a dependency-injection container specialized for AI : it holds the AI services (chat model, embedding model), the plugins (your tools), and the filters, and it orchestrates invocations among them. ┌───────────────────────── Kernel ─────────────────────────┐ Your application ────> │ AI services Plugins Filters Logging │ ────> Model │ (chat, (kernel functions: (approval, telemetry │ providers │ embeddings...) your C# tools) redaction) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ var builder = Kernel . CreateBuilder (); // a builder, similar to a host/service builder builder . AddOpenAIChatCompletion ( "gpt-4o-mini" , apiKey ); // register an AI service builder . Plugins . AddFromType < OrdersPlugin >( "Orders" ); // register a plugin builder . Services . AddLogging ( l => l . AddConsole ()); // the standard .NET service collection is available Kernel kernel = builder . Build (); Core vocabulary Kernel The container/orchestrator holding services, plugins, and filters. KernelFunction One callable unit — either a native C# method or a prompt (Sections 4, 6). KernelPlugin A named group of related kernel functions (Section 3). KernelArguments The named inputs (and execution settings) passed to a function or prompt. FunctionResult What a function returned, with metadata (token usage, etc.). ExecutionSettings Model parameters — temperature, max tokens, function-choice behavior (Section 2). ChatHistory The ordered list of system/user/assistant/tool messages in a conversation. Invoking things // A plain prompt with a variable var arguments = new KernelArguments { [ "topic" ] = "dependency injection" }; FunctionResult result = await kernel . InvokePromptAsync ( "Explain {{$topic}} in one sentence." , arguments ); string text = result . GetValue < string >()!; // A specific function by plugin and name var status = await kernel . InvokeAsync ( "Orders" , "get_order_status" , new () { [ "orderNumber" ] = 10482 }); The Kernel is cheap — create per request A Kernel is a lightweight object. In ASP.NET Core, register it with services.AddKernel() (which makes it TRANSIENT) so each request gets its own instance. That is what lets you attach request-specific plugins (the current user, the current tenant) safely — never share one mutable kernel with per-user state across concurrent requests. Kernel.Clone() copies a kernel when you need a variant. Semantic Kernel and Microsoft.Extensions.AI Microsoft.Extensions.AI ( IChatClient , IEmbeddingGenerator ) is the low-level, provider-neutral abstraction layer (see AI APIs with .NET , Section 13). Semantic Kernel builds on it: SK adds orchestration on top — plugins, prompt templates, filters, memory, and agents. Recent SK versions can use IChatClient / IEmbeddingGenerator services directly, so the two compose rather than compete. 2. AI Services Connectors register models behind uniform interfaces An AI service is a registered model endpoint. Your code depends on the interface ( IChatCompletionService ), not on a specific vendor. var builder = Kernel . CreateBuilder (); // OpenAI builder . AddOpenAIChatCompletion ( modelId : "gpt-4o-mini" , apiKey : openAiKey ); // Azure OpenAI — uses the DEPLOYMENT name (see AI APIs with .NET, Section 3) builder . AddAzureOpenAIChatCompletion ( deploymentName : "my-gpt-deployment" , endpoint : "https://my-resource.openai.azure.com/" , apiKey : azureKey ); // overloads also accept an Entra ID TokenCredential (keyless) Kernel kernel = builder . Build (); The services you'll use Chat completion IChatCompletionService — conversational models (the workhorse) Embeddings Text-embedding generation for RAG and memory (registered via AddOpenAI...Embedding... methods; the exact builder method names changed as SK moved to Microsoft.Extensions.AI's IEmbeddingGenerator — check your version) Text to image / audio Image generation, speech-to-text, text-to-speech connectors Using the chat service directly IChatCompletionService chat = kernel . GetRequiredService < IChatCompletionService >(); var history = new ChatHistory (); history . AddSystemMessage ( "You are a concise C# tutor." ); history . AddUserMessage ( "What is a record?" ); ChatMessageContent reply = await chat . GetChatMessageContentAsync ( history , kernel : kernel ); history . AddAssistantMessage ( reply . Content !); // YOU keep the conversation (models are stateless) // Streaming await foreach ( StreamingChatMessageContent chunk in chat . GetStreamingChatMessageContentsAsync ( history , kernel : kernel )) Console . Write ( chunk . Content ); Execution settings: model parameters per call var settings = new OpenAIPromptExecutionSettings { Temperature = 0.2 , MaxTokens = 500 , TopP = 1.0 , FunctionChoiceBehavior = FunctionChoiceBehavior . Auto (), // let the model call plugins (Section 5) }; Settings mean what they mean in AI APIs with .NET , Section 9: low temperature for factual tasks, a token cap to bound cost and length. Provider-specific settings classes exist (for OpenAI/Azure OpenAI, Ollama, Hugging Face, and others); check what your model supports, since some reasoning models restrict parameters like temperature. Multiple models and routing by ServiceId builder . AddOpenAIChatCompletion ( "gpt-4o" , apiKey , serviceId : "smart" ); // strong, expensive builder . AddOpenAIChatCompletion ( "gpt-4o-mini" , apiKey , serviceId : "fast" ); // cheap, quick // Choose per invocation var cheap = new OpenAIPromptExecutionSettings { ServiceId = "fast" }; await kernel . InvokePromptAsync ( "Classify this ticket: {{$text}}" , new ( cheap ) { [ "text" ] = ticketText }); Registering several services under IDs is how SK supports the model routing pattern from LLM Application Development , Section 9: send easy work to a small model and hard work to a stronger one, without changing the calling code. Providers and local models Beyond OpenAI and Azure OpenAI, SK offers connectors for other providers and for local models (for example through Ollama or ONNX). Connector maturity varies — some are stable, others are preview — so check the status of the one you plan to depend on. Structured output The OpenAI connector can constrain responses to a C# type (via a ResponseFormat setting that accepts a type), generating the JSON Schema for you — the SK equivalent of structured outputs in AI APIs with .NET , Section 7. As always, a schema guarantees shape , not truth : validate the values. 3. Plugins A plugin is a group of capabilities you expose to the model A plugin is a named collection of kernel functions — typically a C# class whose methods the model may call. This is how an LLM gets "hands": looking up data, calling your services, performing actions. using System.ComponentModel ; using Microsoft.SemanticKernel ; public class OrdersPlugin ( IOrderService orders , ICurrentUser user ) // dependencies via normal DI { [ KernelFunction ( "get_order_status" )] [ Description ( "Gets the status of one of the CURRENT customer's orders, given its order number." )] public async Task < string > GetOrderStatusAsync ( [ Description ( "The order number, for example 10482" )] int orderNumber , CancellationToken ct = default ) { // Authorization is enforced HERE, in code, using the authenticated user — never trusted to the model var order = await orders . GetForUserAsync ( user . Id , orderNumber , ct ); return order is null ? $"No order { orderNumber } was found for this customer." : $"Order { order . Number } : { order . Status } . Last updated { order . UpdatedOn : d } ." ; } [ KernelFunction ( "cancel_order" )] [ Description ( "Cancels one of the current customer's orders. This is irreversible." )] public async Task < string > CancelOrderAsync ([ Description ( "The order number" )] int orderNumber , CancellationToken ct = default ) => await orders . CancelAsync ( user . Id , orderNumber , ct ) ? "The order was cancelled." : "The order could not be cancelled." ; } Registering plugins // With the builder (the plugin is created via DI, so its constructor dependencies resolve) builder . Plugins . AddFromType < OrdersPlugin >( "Orders" ); // Or add to an existing kernel kernel . Plugins . AddFromType < OrdersPlugin >( "Orders" ); // An already-constructed instance (handy for per-request state) kernel . Plugins . AddFromObject ( new OrdersPlugin ( orders , currentUser ), "Orders" ); Where plugins come from NATIVE CODE C# classes with [KernelFunction] methods (above). The most common source. PROMPTS Prompt functions defined in code, YAML, or files (Section 6). OPENAPI Import a REST API from its OpenAPI/Swagger spec — each operation becomes a function (kernel.ImportPluginFromOpenApiAsync...). Fast for existing APIs; review which operations you actually expose. MCP Model Context Protocol servers can be exposed as plugins, letting the model use the growing ecosystem of MCP tools (check current connector status). BUILT-IN Core plugins (time, text helpers, etc.) — convenient, but review what you expose. Designing plugins well - THE DESCRIPTIONS ARE THE API. The model decides when and how to call a function from its name, its [Description], and its parameter descriptions. Write them like documentation for a new colleague: what it does, when to use it, what the arguments mean, and any limits. - SMALL, FOCUSED, WELL-NAMED functions beat a few giant ones. Use clear verbs (get_order_status). - LEAST PRIVILEGE. Expose only what the scenario needs. Every function you add is something a prompt-injected or confused model could call. - SEPARATE READ FROM WRITE. Reads are low risk; writes and irreversible actions (cancel, send, delete, pay) deserve confirmation (Section 5) and clear warnings in their descriptions. - RETURN SMALL, USEFUL TEXT. Whatever the function returns goes back into the model's context window and counts as tokens. Return the few fields needed, not an entire database record. - ENFORCE AUTHORIZATION IN CODE using the authenticated user (as above). Never let the model supply "which user am I acting as" as a parameter. - VALIDATE ARGUMENTS like any untrusted input — they come from a model steered by user text. Use parameterized queries; never concatenate them into SQL or shell commands. - RETURN HELPFUL ERRORS AS TEXT ("No order 123 found for this customer") so the model can recover or explain, instead of throwing opaque exceptions. 4. Functions Kernel functions: the unit everything else is built from A KernelFunction is a callable unit with a name, a description, typed parameters, and a result. There are two kinds, and both are invoked the same way and can both be offered to the model. Native functions — your C# code public class TextPlugin { [ KernelFunction ( "word_count" )] [ Description ( "Counts the words in a piece of text." )] public int WordCount ([ Description ( "The text to count" )] string text ) => text . Split ( ' ' , StringSplitOptions . RemoveEmptyEntries ). Length ; } Method parameters can include a Kernel (to call other functions or services from inside), a CancellationToken , and a KernelArguments , none of which the model sees. Return types can be simple values, strings, or objects that SK serializes to JSON for the model. Prompt functions — a prompt that behaves like a function KernelFunction summarize = kernel . CreateFunctionFromPrompt ( promptTemplate : "Summarize the following text in {{$sentences}} sentences:\n\n{{$input}}" , functionName : "summarize" , description : "Summarizes text to a requested number of sentences." ); var result = await kernel . InvokeAsync ( summarize , new () { [ "input" ] = articleText , [ "sentences" ] = 2 }); A prompt function is a prompt template plus execution settings, wrapped as a function . That uniformity is powerful: because prompts and code are both kernel functions, they compose — a prompt can call native code, native code can call a prompt, and the model can be offered either as a tool. Calling functions directly vs. letting the model call them // 1. YOU decide (deterministic): call a function explicitly var count = await kernel . InvokeAsync ( "Text" , "word_count" , new () { [ "text" ] = "one two three" }); // 2. The MODEL decides (function calling — Section 5): offered as tools; the model chooses Prefer DIRECT, explicit calls when the sequence of steps is known — it is cheaper, faster, testable, and predictable. Let the model choose tools only for the parts that genuinely need open-ended judgment. (This is the "workflow vs. agent" distinction from LLM Application Development, Section 11.) Function results and metadata FunctionResult r = await kernel . InvokePromptAsync ( "Say hello" ); string ? text = r . GetValue < string >(); var metadata = r . Metadata ; // provider metadata, such as token usage — log it for cost tracking 5. Function Calling Semantic Kernel runs the tool-calling loop for you In AI APIs with .NET , Section 6, you wrote the loop by hand: send tool definitions, receive tool calls, run them, send results back, repeat. Semantic Kernel does exactly that automatically when you enable function calling. 1. SK converts each registered kernel function (name, description, parameter schema from your C# types) into the tool definitions the model understands. 2. The model replies with a request to call a function (name + JSON arguments). 3. SK deserializes the arguments, invokes your C# method, and appends the result to the chat history. 4. SK calls the model again with the results — repeating until the model produces a final answer. var settings = new OpenAIPromptExecutionSettings { FunctionChoiceBehavior = FunctionChoiceBehavior . Auto () // offer all kernel functions; auto-invoke the chosen ones }; var history = new ChatHistory ( "You are a helpful customer-support assistant for ACME." ); history . AddUserMessage ( "What's the status of order 10482?" ); IChatCompletionService chat = kernel . GetRequiredService < IChatCompletionService >(); ChatMessageContent reply = await chat . GetChatMessageContentAsync ( history , settings , kernel ); // pass the kernel! Console . WriteLine ( reply . Content ); Passing the kernel is what gives the chat service access to your plugins. Function choice behaviors FunctionChoiceBehavior.Auto() The model decides whether and which functions to call; SK invokes them automatically (the default pattern). FunctionChoiceBehavior.Required() The model MUST call a function (useful to force structured extraction or a specific action). FunctionChoiceBehavior.None() Functions are described to the model but it cannot call them. Restrict WHICH functions are offered: FunctionChoiceBehavior.Auto(functions: [kernel.Plugins.GetFunction("Orders", "get_order_status")]) — offer only the functions relevant to this request; fewer tools means fewer mistakes, less risk, and fewer input tokens. Manual invocation: FunctionChoiceBehavior.Auto(autoInvoke: false) — the model's tool-call requests are returned to YOUR code, so you can inspect, approve, or run them yourself, then continue the conversation. Filters: your control point over every call Because SK sits in the loop, it can offer filters — middleware that wraps function invocations. This is where you put logging, authorization, approval gates, redaction, and limits. // Wraps EVERY function invocation (whether chosen by the model or called directly) public class ToolAuditAndApprovalFilter ( IApprovalService approvals , ILogger < ToolAuditAndApprovalFilter > logger ) : IFunctionInvocationFilter { private static readonly HashSet < string > NeedsApproval = [ "Orders.cancel_order" ]; public async Task OnFunctionInvocationAsync ( FunctionInvocationContext context , Func < FunctionInvocationContext , Task > next ) { string name = $" { context . Function . PluginName } . { context . Function . Name } " ; if ( NeedsApproval . Contains ( name ) && ! await approvals . IsApprovedAsync ( name , context . Arguments )) { // Short-circuit: the real function never runs; the model is told why context . Result = new FunctionResult ( context . Function , "The user did not approve this action." ); return ; } var sw = Stopwatch . StartNew (); await next ( context ); // run the function (and any inner filters) logger . LogInformation ( "Tool {Tool} completed in {Ms} ms" , name , sw . ElapsedMilliseconds ); } } builder . Services . AddSingleton < IFunctionInvocationFilter , ToolAuditAndApprovalFilter >(); // Cap how many tool-calling rounds the model can run inside one request public class MaxToolRoundsFilter : IAutoFunctionInvocationFilter { public async Task OnAutoFunctionInvocationAsync ( AutoFunctionInvocationContext context , Func < AutoFunctionInvocationContext , Task > next ) { if ( context . RequestSequenceIndex >= 5 ) // the 6th round: stop { context . Terminate = true ; // end the auto-invocation loop return ; } await next ( context ); } } Filter types: IFunctionInvocationFilter wraps any function invocation: audit, approve, handle errors, redact results IAutoFunctionInvocationFilter specific to the model-driven loop: cap rounds, terminate early, inspect the sequence of calls IPromptRenderFilter runs after a prompt template renders and before it's sent: inspect or redact the final prompt (PII scrubbing, logging, safety checks) Safety rules — identical to hand-rolled tool calling - The model PROPOSES calls; your code and filters decide what actually runs. That is the security boundary. - VALIDATE arguments and ENFORCE AUTHORIZATION inside the function, using the authenticated user. - REQUIRE APPROVAL for irreversible or high-impact actions. - BOUND the loop (round caps, token budgets, timeouts). - Treat tool OUTPUT as untrusted: a function that returns web content or customer text may carry a prompt-injection attempt back into the model's context. - OFFER ONLY the tools a request needs. 6. Prompt Templates Parameterized prompts as first-class, reusable assets A prompt template is prompt text with placeholders and optional function calls, rendered into the final prompt at invocation time. Treating prompts as templates — rather than concatenated strings scattered through code — makes them reusable, testable, and versionable (see LLM Application Development , Section 2). Built-in template syntax {{$variable}} insert an argument: "Explain {{$topic}} for {{$audience}}." {{Plugin.Function}} call a kernel function and insert its result: "Today is {{Time.Today}}." {{Plugin.Function $arg}} call a function with an argument const string prompt = """ You are a support assistant . Today is {{ Time . Today }}. Answer the customer ' s question in a {{ $ tone }} tone . Question : {{ $ question }} """; var result = await kernel . InvokePromptAsync ( prompt , new KernelArguments { [ "tone" ] = "friendly" , [ "question" ] = "Where can I download my invoice?" }); Chat-structured prompts A template can define multiple roles inline, giving the same system/user/assistant structure as a chat request (and making few-shot examples natural): <message role= "system" > You classify support tickets as Billing, Bug, or Feature. Reply with the label only. </message> <message role= "user" > I was charged twice this month. </message> <message role= "assistant" > Billing </message> <message role= "user" > {{$ticket}} </message> Other template languages Semantic Kernel template The default {{$var}} syntax above. Handlebars Adds loops and conditionals ({{#each}}, {{#if}}) — useful for rendering lists of retrieved passages. Requires the Handlebars prompt-template package and TemplateFormat = "handlebars". Liquid Another supported option via its own package. var config = new PromptTemplateConfig { Template = """ Answer using ONLY these sources : {{ # each sources }} [{{ @index }}] {{ this }} {{/ each }} Question : {{ question }} """, TemplateFormat = "handlebars" , Name = "answer_from_sources" , }; KernelFunction fn = kernel . CreateFunctionFromPrompt ( config , new HandlebarsPromptTemplateFactory ()); Prompts as files: keep them out of code Prompts/ Summarizer/ skprompt.txt the template text config.json description, input variables, and execution settings (temperature, max tokens...) KernelPlugin prompts = kernel . CreatePluginFromPromptDirectory ( "Prompts/Summarizer" ); kernel . Plugins . Add ( prompts ); // Or define a prompt function in YAML and load it KernelFunction fromYaml = kernel . CreateFunctionFromPromptYaml ( yamlText ); Storing prompts as files means they live in source control, get reviewed like code, can be changed without recompiling, and can be evaluated against a test set (see RAG , Section 12) — treat them as versioned artifacts. Prompt-injection safety in templates SK ENCODES template variables by default: when {{$userText}} is inserted into a chat-structured prompt, special characters are HTML-encoded so user input can't inject its own <message role="system"> blocks. Leave this on. Only relax it (via the input variable's "allow dangerous content" option) for content you fully trust, and never for user input or retrieved documents. Still: delimit untrusted text clearly, don't rely on encoding as your only defense, and enforce permissions in code (see LLM Application Development, Section 3). Inspect and filter the final prompt An IPromptRenderFilter sees the rendered prompt before it's sent — the right place to log it (carefully, since it may contain personal data), scrub PII, or block requests that violate policy. 7. Memory "Memory" in Semantic Kernel spans several different things. Distinguishing them avoids a lot of confusion — and the area has changed more than any other, so check current docs. 1. CHAT HISTORY Short-term: the messages of the current conversation (ChatHistory). 2. VECTOR STORES Long-term/semantic: embeddings stored and searched for retrieval (RAG, user memories). 3. LEGACY MEMORY APIs Older "SemanticTextMemory"/Memory-plugin abstractions — superseded; avoid in new code. Short-term memory: ChatHistory var history = new ChatHistory ( "You are a helpful assistant." ); // system message history . AddUserMessage ( userInput ); var reply = await chat . GetChatMessageContentAsync ( history , settings , kernel ); history . AddAssistantMessage ( reply . Content !); The model is stateless, so ChatHistory is how your app "remembers": you resend it each turn. That has the cost and context-window consequences covered in AI APIs with .NET , Section 8 — so you must bound it . Persisting: a ChatHistory can be serialized to JSON, so store it (database, cache) keyed by conversation ID — don't keep it in server memory if you scale out or restart. Bounding it: SK includes chat-history REDUCERS — components that truncate old messages or summarize them (check the current names, such as truncation and summarization reducers) — implementing the sliding-window and summarization strategies from LLM Application Development, Section 10. Or trim it yourself before each call. Long-term memory: vector store abstractions Semantic Kernel (together with Microsoft.Extensions.VectorData ) provides a vector store abstraction : you describe a record type with attributes, and connectors implement it over Azure AI Search, PostgreSQL (pgvector), Redis, MongoDB, Qdrant, an in-memory store for tests, and others — the same stores covered in this series' Embeddings & Vector Search guide. // ⚠ Attribute and method names in this area have been renamed across releases // (earlier previews used VectorStoreRecord* attribute names). Match your installed version. public sealed class DocChunk { [ VectorStoreKey ] public string Id { get ; set ; } = "" ; [ VectorStoreData ( IsIndexed = true )] // filterable (e.g. tenant isolation) public int TenantId { get ; set ; } [ VectorStoreData ] public string Source { get ; set ; } = "" ; [ VectorStoreData ] public string Text { get ; set ; } = "" ; [ VectorStoreVector ( 1536 , DistanceFunction = DistanceFunction . CosineSimilarity )] public ReadOnlyMemory < float > Embedding { get ; set ; } } var collection = vectorStore . GetCollection < string , DocChunk >( "docs" ); await collection . EnsureCollectionExistsAsync (); await collection . UpsertAsync ( chunk ); await foreach ( var hit in collection . SearchAsync ( queryEmbedding , top : 5 , new VectorSearchOptions < DocChunk > { Filter = c => c . TenantId == tenantId })) { Console . WriteLine ( $" { hit . Score : F3 } { hit . Record . Text } " ); } The value of the abstraction is portability : prototype against the in-memory connector, then switch to Azure AI Search or pgvector by changing registration, not retrieval code. The cost is that you're limited to the common feature set, and store-specific capabilities (rich hybrid search, tuning) may need the native SDK — a trade-off to weigh against hand-writing a thin IChunkStore interface as in the RAG guide. Long-term user memory (facts across conversations) Same pattern as "Long-term memory" in LLM Application Development, Section 10: extract durable facts after conversations, store them (with embeddings) in a vector store, retrieve the relevant few on each request, and inject them into the prompt. Keep the same discipline: store durable facts rather than transcripts, give users visibility and deletion, isolate memories strictly per user/tenant, and treat stored memories as untrusted data. Legacy memory APIs Older SK versions had a "semantic memory" abstraction ( SemanticTextMemory , ISemanticTextMemory , a Text Memory plugin). Those have been superseded by the vector store abstractions above, and tutorials using them are common and outdated — prefer the vector store approach in new code. 8. Agents An agent: a model + instructions + tools, managing its own conversation Semantic Kernel's Agent Framework builds on the kernel to provide agents as first-class objects: you give an agent a name , instructions (its system prompt), a kernel (its plugins and AI service), and it runs the think → call tools → observe loop, with a managed conversation thread . (The concept of an agent and its loop is in LLM Application Development , Section 11.) using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Agents ; ChatCompletionAgent supportAgent = new () { Name = "SupportAgent" , Instructions = """ You are a customer - support agent for ACME . Use the Orders tools to look up information ; never guess order details . If a request is outside orders and shipping , politely say you can ' t help with it . """, Kernel = kernel , // the agent's AI service and plugins Arguments = new KernelArguments ( new OpenAIPromptExecutionSettings { FunctionChoiceBehavior = FunctionChoiceBehavior . Auto () }), }; // A thread holds the conversation state across turns ChatHistoryAgentThread thread = new (); await foreach ( var response in supportAgent . InvokeAsync ( new ChatMessageContent ( AuthorRole . User , "Where is my order 10482?" ), thread )) { Console . WriteLine ( response . Message . Content ); } ⚠ The agent APIs are among the fastest-moving parts of SK: the shape of InvokeAsync , the thread types, and the names of response objects have changed between releases, and parts of the framework are marked experimental. The concepts — name, instructions, kernel/tools, thread, invoke — are stable; verify exact signatures against your installed version. Agent types ChatCompletionAgent Runs on any chat-completion service you register (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, local models) and manages the loop and plugins in YOUR process. The general-purpose choice. OpenAIAssistantAgent Wraps OpenAI's server-side Assistants capabilities (hosted threads, built-in tools such as code interpreter and file search). State and tool execution live in the service. Azure AI agents Wrap Azure's hosted agent service (Azure AI Foundry Agent Service) — managed threads, tools, and enterprise controls on Azure. Threads and state Agent THREAD = the conversation the agent is having. With ChatCompletionAgent you hold the thread (and thus the history) in your application and must persist and bound it exactly like ChatHistory. Hosted agent types keep thread state in the service instead — which changes where your data lives, what you can delete, and how you meet your compliance obligations. Choose deliberately. Agents inherit every risk of tool-using systems Everything from the function-calling section applies, amplified by autonomy: least-privilege plugins, authorization in code, approval filters for consequential actions, round and token caps, treating tool output as untrusted, and full logging of every step (see LLM Application Development, Section 11). Use the simplest design that works: a single prompt, then a fixed workflow, then function calling, and an agent only when the task genuinely needs open-ended multi-step decisions. 9. Planning What "planning" means — and what happened to the planners Planning is deciding which steps to take, in what order to achieve a goal. Early versions of Semantic Kernel shipped dedicated planner classes (such as sequential, stepwise, and Handlebars planners): a planner asked the model to produce a multi-step plan from the available functions, then executed it. Those standalone planners have since been DEPRECATED and removed in favor of FUNCTION CALLING. Modern models are trained to plan implicitly through tool use — they call a function, read the result, decide what to do next, and continue — so SK's recommended "planner" is simply: FunctionChoiceBehavior.Auto() + well-described plugins + an iteration cap Older articles and samples that mention HandlebarsPlanner , FunctionCallingStepwisePlanner , or similar are describing an earlier era; modern SK code gets the same capability from automatic function calling, with less machinery, fewer extra model calls, and better results. Planning with function calling var kernel = builder . Build (); // plugins: Calendar, Email, Orders... var settings = new OpenAIPromptExecutionSettings { FunctionChoiceBehavior = FunctionChoiceBehavior . Auto () }; // One request that needs SEVERAL steps — the model plans them as it goes: // 1. look up the order 2. check the delivery date 3. draft an email 4. add a calendar reminder var result = await kernel . InvokePromptAsync ( "Find the delivery date for order 10482, email the customer an update, and set a reminder the day before." , new ( settings )); Planning patterns you control IMPLICIT (function calling loop) The model plans one step at a time as it works. Flexible and simple; harder to predict, and only as reliable as the model and your tool design. EXPLICIT PLAN-THEN-EXECUTE Step 1: ask the model to produce a PLAN as structured output (a typed list of steps, validated against your allowed actions). Step 2: your code reviews and executes the steps — optionally after human approval. More predictable and auditable, at the cost of flexibility and one extra call. FIXED WORKFLOW You decide the sequence in code and use the model only inside each step (classify -> retrieve -> draft -> validate). The most reliable option when the steps are known in advance — prefer it whenever you can. HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP Approval filters or manual function invocation (autoInvoke: false) pause for confirmation before consequential steps. Keeping planning bounded - CAP the number of tool-calling rounds (the MaxToolRoundsFilter in Section 5). - Set a TOKEN and TIME budget per request; cancel via CancellationToken. - Offer a SMALL, relevant set of functions per request — a model choosing among 5 tools plans better than among 50, and it costs fewer input tokens. - Write functions to be IDEMPOTENT and to return clear errors, so a retry or a wrong turn is recoverable. - LOG the full sequence of calls so you can see what the model decided and why. - Plans can be WRONG: validate each step's arguments and authorization at execution time, not at planning time. 10. Multi-Agent Systems Several specialized agents collaborating A multi-agent system divides a problem among agents with different roles, instructions, and tools — for example an analyst , a writer , and a reviewer — coordinated so their work combines into a result. Why split work among agents? - SPECIALIZATION: focused instructions and a small toolset per agent are easier to get right than one do-everything prompt. - SEPARATION OF CONCERNS: a reviewer agent can critique a writer agent's output with a different "mindset." - PARALLELISM: independent sub-tasks can run at the same time. - MODULARITY: agents can be developed, tested, and swapped independently. Why NOT? - Every agent boundary adds model calls, latency, and cost, and new failure modes (miscommunication, loops, error compounding). Start with ONE agent or a plain workflow; add agents only when a single one demonstrably struggles. Orchestration patterns Semantic Kernel's agent framework offers orchestration abstractions that implement common coordination patterns over a set of agents (these are newer and flagged experimental in places — check current status): SEQUENTIAL A pipeline: each agent's output is the next agent's input. researcher -> writer -> reviewer CONCURRENT The same task goes to several agents in parallel; results are gathered and combined. GROUP CHAT Agents take turns in a shared conversation, with a manager deciding who speaks next and when to stop. HANDOFF One agent hands the conversation to another better suited to the request (triage -> billing -> tech). MAGENTIC A manager agent plans and delegates a complex, open-ended task to specialist agents dynamically. // A sequential pipeline: research -> write -> review ChatCompletionAgent researcher = new () { Name = "Researcher" , Instructions = "Gather the key facts on the topic." , Kernel = kernel }; ChatCompletionAgent writer = new () { Name = "Writer" , Instructions = "Write a clear 3-paragraph summary from the facts." , Kernel = kernel }; ChatCompletionAgent reviewer = new () { Name = "Reviewer" , Instructions = "Check the draft for errors; return a corrected final version." , Kernel = kernel }; SequentialOrchestration orchestration = new ( researcher , writer , reviewer ); InProcessRuntime runtime = new (); await runtime . StartAsync (); OrchestrationResult < string > result = await orchestration . InvokeAsync ( "The benefits of dependency injection" , runtime ); string final = await result . GetValueAsync ( TimeSpan . FromSeconds ( 120 )); // always bound the wait await runtime . RunUntilIdleAsync (); (Earlier SK versions offered an AgentGroupChat class for group conversations; the orchestration patterns above are the newer direction. Check your version's documentation.) A simpler multi-agent pattern: agents as tools Instead of a full orchestration, wrap a SUB-AGENT as a kernel function on a main agent's kernel — a "research" function whose implementation invokes a research agent and returns its answer. The main agent then delegates by ordinary function calling. This keeps the control flow understandable (one agent in charge, others as specialist tools), and it reuses everything from Section 5, including filters for logging and approval. Controlling multi-agent systems - BOUND EVERYTHING: max turns, max total tokens, wall-clock timeouts. Agents can talk in circles. - LEAST PRIVILEGE PER AGENT: give each only its own tools — the reviewer needn't send email. - DEFINE TERMINATION: an explicit "done" condition, not "until they stop talking." - LOG THE TRANSCRIPT between agents; it's your only way to debug emergent behavior. - BEWARE COMPOUNDING ERRORS AND COST: an early mistake propagates, and N agents multiply token spend. - EVALUATE end to end on a test set (see RAG, Section 12) — multi-agent behavior is hard to judge by eye. - Consider whether a deterministic workflow with a verification step would do the job more reliably. Semantic Kernel and the Microsoft Agent Framework For new agent-centric and multi-agent work, evaluate the Microsoft Agent Framework , which Microsoft positions as the next-generation framework from the Semantic Kernel and AutoGen teams, with agent abstractions and graph-based workflows. Semantic Kernel remains a mature option, especially for applications built around plugins, prompt templates, and function calling. Check the current status, feature parity, and migration guidance (Section 13) before committing. 11. RAG with Semantic Kernel Everything in this series' RAG guide — ingestion, chunking, embedding, retrieval, filtering, reranking, grounded prompts, citation validation, evaluation — still applies. The tenant-isolation point Notice that tenantId is a CONSTRUCTOR argument of the plugin — NOT a parameter the model supplies. The model never chooses whose documents to search; the application binds the plugin to the authenticated user's scope on a per-request kernel. Built-in text-search and vector-store helpers SK also provides text search abstractions that wrap a vector store or a web search engine as a searchable source and can expose it to the model as a plugin (or to a prompt template for retrieval-in-template patterns), with connectors for stores such as Azure AI Search. Hand-written retrieval, as above, gives maximum control when quality and security matter most. What doesn't change SK does not make retrieval good — the work from the RAG guide still decides quality: - extraction and chunking quality - hybrid search and reranking - metadata captured at ingestion - a score threshold and an explicit "not found" path - citation validation - evaluation: Recall@k/MRR for retrieval, faithfulness for generation Frameworks reduce plumbing; they don't reduce the need to measure. 12. RequireRateLimiting ( "ai" ); // see AI APIs with .NET, Section 11 public record ChatRequest ( string ConversationId , string Message ); Operational concerns OBSERVABILITY SK emits logs, metrics, and OpenTelemetry traces for model calls and function invocations. Wire them into your telemetry pipeline. Capturing full prompts and responses in traces is a sensitive opt-in (they can contain personal data) — enable it deliberately and protect where it goes. RESILIENCE Model calls still need timeouts, retries with jittered backoff, rate limiting, and cost caps (see AI APIs with .NET, Sections 10-12) — frameworks don't remove them. COST Log token usage from function results; cap rounds and output tokens; route easy work to a small model with ServiceId; cache repeated work. TESTING Test plugins as ordinary C# classes (they're just methods). Test prompts with an evaluation set. Use a fake chat service for deterministic tests of orchestration code. CONFIGURATION Model names, deployment names, and prices in configuration, not code. 13. Semantic Kernel vs. the Alternatives The layers of the .NET AI stack RAW PROVIDER SDK OpenAI / Azure.AI.OpenAI packages. Maximum control, no abstraction, you write the tool loop, history handling, and plumbing yourself. Microsoft.Extensions.AI Small, provider-neutral abstractions (IChatClient, IEmbeddingGenerator) plus middleware for logging, caching, telemetry, and automatic function invocation. A thin, stable foundation. SEMANTIC KERNEL Orchestration on top: plugins, prompt templates (Handlebars/YAML/files), filters, vector-store abstractions, agents, multi-agent orchestration, observability. MICROSOFT AGENT The newer framework from the SK and AutoGen teams focused on agents and workflows FRAMEWORK (including graph-based, multi-step workflows). Evaluate it for new agent-centric work. Choosing A few model calls, simple tools, you value minimal dependencies -> raw SDK or Microsoft.Extensions.AI. Don't adopt a framework for a single chat completion. A plugin-based assistant, reusable prompt assets, filters for governance, model routing, tidy DI integration -> Semantic Kernel. Autonomous agents, complex multi-agent workflows, long-running orchestrations -> evaluate the Microsoft Agent Framework alongside SK's agent framework; check current maturity and migration guidance. A fixed, well-understood RAG pipeline where you want full control over every stage -> plain C# services (as in the RAG guide), optionally using SK for templating, filters, and the generation step. Honest trade-offs of using a framework GAINS Less boilerplate; consistent patterns for tools, prompts, and filters; provider portability; built-in observability; a shared vocabulary for teams. COSTS A dependency that changes fast (renames, experimental APIs, deprecations — plan for upgrade effort); abstractions can obscure what is actually sent to the model, so inspect prompts and token usage; the common-denominator API may lag provider-specific features; more moving parts to debug. MITIGATE Keep your domain logic (plugins, retrieval, validation) in plain C# classes behind your own interfaces so the framework is a thin layer you could replace; pin versions and read release notes; log the real prompts (carefully); and keep an evaluation set so framework upgrades don't silently change behavior. 14. Common Pitfalls Pitfall Why it hurts Better approach Following outdated tutorials (old planners, legacy memory, early agent APIs) The API has been renamed and reorganized repeatedly; old samples don't compile or are deprecated Check the docs for your installed version; use function calling instead of planners and vector stores instead of legacy memory (Sections 7, 9) Sharing one Kernel with per-user plugins across requests State leaks between concurrent users Use AddKernel() (transient) or Clone() per request; bind plugins to the current user (Sections 1, 11) Vague plugin and function descriptions The model picks the wrong tool or never uses it Write names and descriptions like API documentation (Section 3) Giving the model a userId / tenantId parameter The model (or an injected prompt) can act as someone else Bind identity at plugin construction from authentication; enforce authorization in code (Sections 3, 11) Exposing too many tools More mistakes, more risk, more input tokens Offer a small, relevant set per request (Sections 3, 5) Auto-invoking irreversible actions A confused or injected model cancels orders or sends email Approval filters or autoInvoke: false for high-impact functions (Section 5) Forgetting to pass the kernel to the chat service The model never sees your plugins Pass kernel into GetChatMessageContentAsync (Section 5) No cap on tool-calling rounds Loops burn tokens and money Use an IAutoFunctionInvocationFilter round cap, token budgets, and timeouts (Sections 5, 9) Unbounded ChatHistory Cost and latency grow until the context window overflows Persist externally and bound it with reducers, windowing, or summarization (Section 7) Trusting tool and retrieved content Hidden instructions in documents or web results can hijack the model Treat all tool output as untrusted data; delimit it; limit privileges (Sections 5, 6, 11) Disabling template-variable encoding for user input Lets users inject their own system messages into chat-structured prompts Leave encoding on; relax only for trusted content (Section 6) Building a multi-agent system by default More calls, latency, cost, and failure modes for no demonstrated gain Start with one agent or a workflow; add agents only when needed (Section 10) Letting agents converse without limits They loop, drift, and rack up cost Max turns, token and time budgets, explicit termination conditions (Section 10) Assuming the framework fixes RAG quality Retrieval quality depends on chunking, metadata, hybrid search, reranking, and evaluation Do the RAG work; measure Recall@k and faithfulness (Section 11) Never inspecting the real prompts and token usage The abstraction hides what is sent; costs and bugs surprise you Use render filters and telemetry to see actual prompts and usage (Sections 6, 12) Binding business logic tightly to the framework Rapid API churn makes upgrades painful Keep logic in plain C# behind your own interfaces; pin versions (Section 13) Hard-coding model names and keys Rotations, deployments, and upgrades require code changes Configuration and secrets stores; ServiceId for routing (Section 2) Quick Reference Table Concept API / idea Purpose Kernel Kernel.CreateBuilder() … Build() / services.AddKernel() Container + orchestrator for services, plugins, and filters AI service AddOpenAIChatCompletion(...) / AddAzureOpenAIChatCompletion(...) Register a model behind a uniform interface Chat service kernel.GetRequiredService<IChatCompletionService>() Run chat completions with a ChatHistory Multiple models serviceId: + PromptExecutionSettings.ServiceId Route work to cheap or strong models Execution settings OpenAIPromptExecutionSettings { Temperature, MaxTokens, ... } Model parameters and function-choice behavior Plugin Class with [KernelFunction] methods; Plugins.AddFromType<T>() Expose C# code to the model Descriptions [Description("...")] on functions and parameters How the model decides when and how to call a tool Kernel function Native method or prompt function The unit of invocation; composable Direct invoke kernel.InvokeAsync("Plugin", "function", args) Deterministic, explicit call Function calling FunctionChoiceBehavior.Auto() SK runs the model↔tool loop for you Manual control Auto(autoInvoke: false) / Required() / None() Approve calls, force a call, or disable calls Filters IFunctionInvocationFilter , IAutoFunctionInvocationFilter , IPromptRenderFilter Audit, approve, cap, redact, log Prompt template {{$var}} , {{Plugin.Function}} , Handlebars, YAML, prompt files Reusable, versionable, parameterized prompts Chat history ChatHistory (+ reducers) Short-term conversation memory Vector store Microsoft.Extensions.VectorData abstractions + connectors Long-term/semantic memory and RAG storage Agent ChatCompletionAgent { Name, Instructions, Kernel } + thread Tool-using assistant managing its own loop Planning Function calling + caps (planners deprecated) Multi-step goal pursuit Multi-agent Sequential / Concurrent / GroupChat / Handoff / Magentic orchestration Coordinate specialist agents RAG Retrieve in code → prompt template, or search as a plugin Grounded answers with SK's templating and filters Conclusion Semantic Kernel is best understood as the .NET plumbing for the patterns this series has already covered: a Kernel that holds your AI services, plugins, and filters; plugins that expose C# code to the model; function calling that runs the model-and-tool loop for you; prompt templates that turn prompts into reusable, versionable assets; memory in the form of chat history and vector-store abstractions; and agents and orchestration for work that needs autonomy or specialization. Because it fits .NET idioms — dependency injection, configuration, logging, attributes, filters — it can make AI features feel like the rest of your application rather than a bolted-on script. The principles that keep it safe and reliable are the same ones that governed hand-written tool calling, and a framework doesn't relax them: the model proposes while your code decides, so enforce authorization and validation inside functions and bind identity from authentication rather than from model-supplied arguments; require approval for irreversible actions; cap rounds, tokens, and time; treat tool output and retrieved text as untrusted; and choose the simplest architecture that works — a prompt, then a workflow, then function calling, and an agent or multi-agent system only when the problem truly demands it. Retrieval quality still comes from the RAG fundamentals, and quality in general still comes from measurement. Finally, be clear-eyed about the framework itself. Semantic Kernel evolves quickly — planners were replaced by function calling, memory moved to vector-store abstractions, agent and orchestration APIs are still settling, and the Microsoft Agent Framework now sits alongside it for agent-centric work. Keep your domain logic in plain C# behind your own interfaces, pin versions, read release notes, inspect the prompts that are really sent, and keep an evaluation set so upgrades don't silently change behavior. Do that, and Semantic Kernel is a productive, replaceable layer — which is exactly what a framework in a fast-moving field should be. Found this useful? title: What would make you pay for AI cost savings? A 30-line script that shows where your agent tokens go
author: rene
summary: A recent Ask HN asked: "Would you pay for saving AI cost?" and "what would you need to see before trusting to pay?" My answer: a number measured on my own logs, before and after, that I can reproduce. Not a percentage claim from a landing page. So here is the measuring part, free. Run it on your own agent transcripts first; decide about fixes after. Step 1: find where the tokens go Most coding-agent cost is not your prompt. It is repeated context: the same file dumps, tool output and boilerplate resent every turn. This script takes a JSONL transcript (one message per line, with a content string) and reports which chunks repeat the most. // token-hotspots.mjs - node token-hotspots.mjs transcript.jsonl import fs from " node:fs " ; const lines = fs . readFileSync ( process . argv [ 2 ], " utf8 " ). split ( " \n " ). filter ( Boolean ); const approxTokens = s => Math . ceil ( s . length / 4 ); // rough: ~4 chars per token const seen = new Map (); let total = 0 ; for ( const l of lines ) { let m ; try { m = JSON . parse ( l ); } catch { continue ; } const text = typeof m . content === " string " ? m . content : JSON . stringify ( m . content ?? "" ); total += approxTokens ( text ); // fingerprint each 400-char block for ( let i = 0 ; i < text . length ; i += 400 ) { const k = text . slice ( i , i + 400 ); if ( k . length < 200 ) continue ; seen . set ( k , ( seen . get ( k ) || 0 ) + 1 ); } } const repeated = [... seen . entries ()]. filter (([, n ]) => n > 1 ); const wasted = repeated . reduce (( a , [ k , n ]) => a + approxTokens ( k ) * ( n - 1 ), 0 ); console . log ({ messages : lines . length , approxTotalTokens : total , approxRepeatedTokens : wasted , repeatedShare : total ? + ( wasted / total ). toFixed ( 3 ) : 0 }); repeated . sort (( a , b ) => b [ 1 ] - a [ 1 ]). slice ( 0 , 5 ) . forEach (([ k , n ]) => console . log ( ` ${ n } x ${ k . slice ( 0 , 80 ). replace ( / \n /g , " " )} ...` )); The repeatedShare number is the ceiling on what a de-duplication pass could save for that transcript. If it is 3%, do not pay anyone. If it is 40%, now you know why. Step 2: the usual fixes, in order of effort Stop re-reading unchanged files. Cache by path + mtime and send a reference instead of the dump. Truncate tool output at the source (tail of test logs, head+tail of long diffs). Pin a short, stable system prompt and move long rules into files loaded on demand. Summarize old turns instead of replaying them. Ask for terse output when you do not need prose. None of these needs a paid tool. The value of a paid checklist is only saving you the hour of working out the order and the thresholds. Honest limits The 4-chars-per-token estimate is rough; use your provider's tokenizer for billing-grade numbers. Repetition share is not the same as savings: some repeats are cached by the provider at a discount, so check your pricing. I have not measured savings across a population of users; run it on yours. If you want the checklist version of the fixes above (with the thresholds and the order I use), it is a pay-what-you-want download, $1 minimum: Prompt Token Diet Checklist . The script above is yours either way. What would you need to see before paying for something like this? I am curious which number convinces you.

title: Meta's Ad Assistant Can Now Build Campaigns From a Chat Prompt — Here's the Approval Playbook
author: MEER
summary: Originally published on DigiHustle On October 6, at Advertising Week New York, Meta announced something more consequential than another AI feature drop. The AI business assistant inside Meta Ads Manager can now plan and create a campaign, generate creative imagery and text, update targeting, and change a budget — conversationally, from a chat prompt. It drafts everything and stages it for your sign-off. Read that again: the assistant executes . For years, "AI in ads" meant a side panel suggesting a headline variant you could accept with one click. This is different. You describe the change in plain language; it builds the campaign, rewrites the creative, shifts the budget, and hands you one job: approve, or don't. Meta says advertisers who act on its recommendations are seeing 5% more conversions at the same cost. Early partner tests compressed campaign launch times by roughly 60%. That's the gap between a tool that advises and a subordinate that acts. What the assistant actually does now Conversational campaign building — describe what you want and the assistant drafts the campaign structure, creative, and settings inside Ads Manager. Creative generation and edits — generates ad imagery and text, and the expanded Ads Creative Studio can now create new video concepts from existing assets. Audience discovery via Customer Lifecycle Strategy — specify acquisition, and the assistant recommends how to exclude existing customers. Conversational budget and targeting changes — "shift $20/day from this ad set to that one" through a prompt. Three things worth letting it do First drafts of video variations from your statics. Brands sitting on 40 product photos while spending $2,000+ on a video shoot for Q4 — Meta's Advantage+ can now generate video from static assets in minutes. Review the first three seconds of each one yourself. The hook is still a human decision. Acquisition exclusions through Customer Lifecycle Strategy. Genuine improvement. Set it up once, verify the exclusions, stop babysitting suppression lists. Creative diagnosis inside Creative Studio. Treat the diagnosis as a starting point for your next brief, not gospel. Two things you never hand over Budget authority. Set your daily cap before prompting the assistant. The assistant doesn't know your cash flow or margin. The assistant proposes budget changes, a human approves every single one. The offer and the brand voice. No assistant can fix a weak offer; it can only dress one up in sharper words. The approval workflow we recommend Monday: Prompt with hard constraints, review every draft against a checklist. Midweek: Generate video/hook variations. Watch the first three seconds of each. Friday: Fatigue check — CTR down 30%+ over two weeks means refresh. Always: Human kill rule. 50% over target CPA for three days = paused by a human. Q4 is the wrong season to learn a new tool by trial and error. Set the guardrails first, then let the machine do the boring parts.

title: Are Mailer Boxes Better for Online Product Shipping? The Structural, Freight, and Fulfillment Blueprint
author: Henry
summary: Mailer boxes are definitively better for direct-to-consumer (D2C) e-commerce, subscription kits, and branded retail products under $15 lbs, whereas traditional Regular Slotted Carton (RSC) shipping boxes remain superior for heavy cargo, bulk wholesale, and industrial fulfillment. By pairing tape-free assembly with high-impact unboxing presentation, custom mailers eliminate fulfillment bottlenecks while safeguarding products across parcel transit networks. MAILER BOXES VS. RSC SHIPPING BOXES CUSTOM CORRUGATED MAILER (RETT) TRADITIONAL SHIPPING BOX (RSC) +---------------------------------+ +---------------------------------+ | Single-piece self-locking clamshell | | Four-flap top/bottom closure | | Tape-free friction tuck design | | Requires top and bottom taping | | Optimized for D2C under 15 lbs | | Engineered for heavy industrial | +---------------------------------+ +---------------------------------+ \ / \ / v [ TOTAL LANDED COST OPTIMIZATION ] - Zero Manual Taping Bottlenecks - Optimized DIM Weight Brackets - Eliminated Transit Damage Rates 1. Introduction Determining whether mailer boxes are better for online product shipping requires an objective comparison of structural physics, packaging mechanics, warehouse fulfillment speeds, and freight economics. For direct-to-consumer (D2C) brands, the Roll End Tuck Top (RETT) corrugated mailer has emerged as the industry standard. However, choosing the wrong box style for your product category creates immediate operational leakage. Failing to align your box architecture with your distribution model leads to severe financial and logistical strain. Industry logistics data confirms that approximately 11% of un-optimized parcel shipments arrive damaged —a metric driven directly by using flimsy paperboard for heavy goods or picking oversized stock shippers that flex under automated sorting conveyor loads. Beyond transit damage, picking the wrong box style creates warehouse fulfillment bottlenecks that slow down packing lines. Worse yet, using oversized packaging triggers carrier Dimensional Weight (DIM) freight surcharges that force your business to pay for transporting empty air. THE HIDDEN COSTS OF MISMATCHED BOX SELECTION INCORRECT CONTAINER SELECTION OPTIMIZED STRUCTURAL ARCHITECTURE +-----------------------------------+ +-----------------------------------+ | 11% Average Transit Breakage Rate | | < 0.5% Verified Damage Rate | | Slow, Manual Fulfillment Assembly | | 50% Faster Packing Line Speeds | | Carrier DIM Weight Freight Penalty| | Lowest Volumetric Freight Tier | | High Material & Void Fill Waste | | Zero Loose Fill Material Required | +-----------------------------------+ +-----------------------------------+ Modern online shipping requires balancing rigorous transit protection with unboxing brand impact. This guide provides a rigorous, data-driven comparison of mailers versus traditional shipping boxes across structural physics, freight economics, and brand impact. 2. Core Baseline Headings Heading 2A: Structural Comparison: Roll End Tuck Top (RETT) Mailers vs. Regular Slotted Cartons (RSCs) Navigating e-commerce packaging requires understanding the structural mechanics that separate custom mailers from traditional industrial shipping boxes. STRUCTURAL ARCHITECTURE COMPARISON ROLL END TUCK TOP (RETT) REGULAR SLOTTED CARTON (RSC) +------------------------------+ +------------------------------+ | Single-piece clamshell dieline| | Four-flap slotted container | | Double-walled side panels | | Requires top/bottom tape | | Friction-fit front tuck tabs | | Industrial bulk stacking | +------------------------------+ +------------------------------+ Roll End Tuck Top (RETT) Mailer Architecture The RETT mailer is a single-piece, self-locking clamshell container engineered with double-walled side panels, internal dust flaps, and front friction tabs. When folded, the side panels roll inward to create double-thickness sidewalls that absorb lateral compression. The front lid locks securely into the base frame without requiring exterior packing tape, creating a clean outer surface and an unboxing reveal when opened. Regular Slotted Carton (RSC) Shipping Box Architecture The RSC is the traditional industrial workhorse of transport packaging. It features four top and bottom flaps of equal length that meet in the center during assembly. Because its closure flaps do not lock mechanically, RSC boxes require pressure-sensitive adhesive tape or mechanical stitching across both top and bottom seams to secure the contents. Assembly Speed & Labor Effort Analysis Fulfillment velocity depends heavily on box architecture. Pre-scored fold lines and friction-lock tabs on RETT mailers accelerate manual assembly, allowing packers to square, pack, and lock a mailer in seconds. In contrast, RSC shippers require a multi-step process: squaring the box, taping the bottom flaps, inserting the product and void fill, and applying top sealing tape—doubling labor time. Tamper Evidence and Security RETT Mailers: Secure contents through interlocking side flaps and tuck tabs. While they offer a clean unboxing experience, they do not provide raw tamper-evident seals unless secured with a branded sticker or security label. RSC Shippers: Tape-sealed seams provide immediate visual tamper evidence across parcel transit hubs, making them ideal for high-value industrial goods. Heading 2B: Material Science & Board Flute Physics: Calibrating Crush Strength and Weight The performance of an online shipping container relies on the engineering of its underlying corrugated board substrate. B-Flute ($1/8\text{ in}$ / $3.2\text{ mm}$ Thickness): Delivers thicker cushioning profiles for drop-impact shock absorption in mailers and small shippers ($10\text{ to } 25\text{ lbs}$). C-Flute & Double-Wall (BC-Flute): Delivers maximum vertical stacking strength and column compression resistance, ideal for heavy RSC master cartons ($25+\text{ lbs}$). Corrugated Strength Ratings Demystified The structural capacity of corrugated board is measured using the Edge Crush Test (ECT) , which evaluates the force ($\text{lb/in}$) required to crush a vertical section of board on its edge: 32 ECT Single-Wall: Standard industry rating for custom D2C mailers shipping contents up to $30\text{ lbs}$. 44 to 55 ECT Single-Wall / Double-Wall: Required for heavy industrial RSC shippers and multi-tier palleted warehouse storage. Void Fill and Tare Weight Impact Oversized stock RSC shippers frequently force operations to pack items in excessive void fill (packing peanuts, crumpled kraft paper, or air pillows) to prevent shifting. This excess void fill increases tare weight and inflates package volume. Custom mailers hug exact product dimensions tightly, eliminating loose void fill and lowering shipping costs. 3. Comparison Section: Mailer Boxes vs. Shipping Boxes (RSCs) Evaluation Matrix Logistics carriers bill parcel shipments using Dimensional Weight (DIM Weight)—a volumetric pricing formula that charges for the physical space a package occupies inside a transport vehicle rather than its actual weight on a scale: $$\text{Dimensional Weight (lbs)} = \frac{\text{Length (in)} \times \text{Width (in)} \times \text{Height (in)}}{139}$$ Over-packaging a product in an oversized stock RSC fills the interior with excess void fill and inflates its volumetric footprint. The Deep-Dive Solution Section: 5-Step Strategic Framework — When to Choose Mailer Boxes vs. Shipping Boxes Selecting the ideal container type for your product catalog requires an organized, 5-step evaluation process. 5-STEP CONTAINER SELECTION ROADMAP STEP 1: Audit Product Weight, Dimensions, and Fragility Thresholds [Measure L x W x D, weigh item; pick mailer for <15lbs or RSC for heavy cargo] | v STEP 2: Calculate Carrier Dimensional Weight (DIM Weight) Surcharges [Apply L x W x H / 139 formula to optimize volumetric freight brackets] | v STEP 3: Analyze Packing Line Throughput and Labor Constraints [Pick tape-free RETT mailers for speed or automated RSC case-sealers] | v STEP 4: Request 1:1 Vector CAD Dielines and Apply Prepress Rules [Enforce 0.125" bleeds, set 0.25" safety margins, clear glue flaps of ink] | v STEP 5: Order Physical Prototype Samples and Execute ISTA 1A Drop Testing [Build unprinted white sample, test lock tension, run ISTA 1A drop test] Step 1: Audit Product Weight, Dimensions, and Fragility Thresholds Weigh your product and measure exact outer bounds ($\text{Length} \times \text{Width} \times \text{Depth}$). If the item is under $15\text{ lbs}$ and requires unboxing engagement, select a corrugated mailer box. If it exceeds $15\text{ lbs}$ or requires bulk palletization, select a Regular Slotted Carton (RSC) shipping box. Step 2: Calculate Carrier Dimensional Weight (DIM Weight) Surcharges Apply the carrier volumetric formula to your proposed outer box dimensions: $$\text{Dimensional Weight (lbs)} = \frac{\text{Length (in)} \times \text{Width (in)} \times \text{Height (in)}}{139}$$ Verify that your selected box style optimizes volumetric freight brackets and eliminates paid empty air. Step 3: Analyze Packing Line Throughput and Labor Constraints Review your fulfillment labor workflows. Choose tape-free RETT mailers to eliminate tape gun bottlenecks and speed up manual packing lines, or automated RSC case-sealers for high-volume industrial wholesale lines. Step 4: Request 1:1 Vector CAD Dielines and Apply Prepress Rules Acquire certified CAD dielines (.AI or .PDF format) from your packaging manufacturer. Lock technical dieline layers in Adobe Illustrator and format graphic artwork according to prepress standards: VECTOR PREPRESS LAYOUT STANDARDS ====================================================== <-- Bleed Line (0.125" Outward) ------------------------------------------------------ <-- Cut Line (Spot 100% Magenta) - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - <-- Score/Crease Line (Spot 100% Cyan) +----------------------------------------------------+ | CRITICAL ARTWORK / LOGO (Keep 0.25" Safety Margin) | +----------------------------------------------------+ Bleed Line Enforcement: Extend background fills at least $0.125\text{ in}$ past physical cut lines. Safety Margins: Keep typography, logos, and barcodes at least $0.25\text{ in}$ away from fold and score lines. Glue Flap Knockouts: Keep ink, varnish, and laminations off all glue flaps to ensure structural adhesives bond securely. Color Conversions: Convert screen-based RGB files to CMYK or assign specific Pantone (PMS) spot colors for accurate press runs. Step 5: Order Physical Prototype Samples and Execute ISTA 1A Drop Testing Never approve mass production without inspecting a physical prototype. Order an unprinted structural white sample or digitally printed prototype and run it through a complete pre-production evaluation: Fit & Tension Verification: Test product fitment and confirm tuck flaps and lock tabs close securely without popping open. Barcode Scannability Audit: Verify that printed UPCs and QR codes feature high contrast (solid black vector over a clean white background) for easy scanning. ISTA 1A Transit Testing: Perform a 3-foot multi-angle drop test onto corners, edges, and flat surfaces to confirm the box protects the product through parcel delivery handling. 6. Conclusion Mailer boxes are definitively better for online product shipping when targeting D2C E-Commerce, Subscription Kits, and Branded Goods under $15 lbs, whereas traditional RSC shipping boxes remain essential for heavy cargo and bulk wholesale logistics. Always match your container selection directly to product weight, fulfillment labor speed, and unboxing marketing goals. Strategic Execution Rule: Engineer your online shipping packaging from the product outward—never select an arbitrary stock box size and fill excess volume with loose plastic peanuts. title: How to cite an immutable open data registry from an autonomous agent
author: Inner Ozma
summary: When an autonomous agent asserts a fact about a company, a product, or an API, the assertion is only as good as its provenance. A number scraped from a homepage and paraphrased into a report is unauditable: six weeks later nobody can tell whether the source changed, whether the agent misread it, or whether the figure was ever true. The fix is not "be careful" — it is to anchor every claim to a source that pins its own bytes. The problem with mutable sources Most data on the open web is a moving target. A pricing page, a "supported integrations" list, a status dashboard — each is a live document that changes without notice and carries no record of what it said when your agent read it. When an agent cites such a page, the citation is a promise the agent cannot keep. The page will drift, and the reader who follows the link a month later will find something else. This is the same failure mode that made reproducible builds important: if the artifact is not content-addressed, "it worked on my machine" becomes "it was true when I looked." Content-addressed registries A better primitive is an immutable, digest-pinned dataset : a file that ships with its own cryptographic identity. Each release declares a release_id and an artifact_sha256 ; a reader can re-hash the file and confirm they hold exactly the bytes the publisher signed. If the digest matches, the fact is verifiable; if it does not, the citation is void. There is no ambiguity and no trust required. Sourcey is one such registry. It publishes versioned datasets — an agent-readiness index, a startup-credits catalogue, a companies file, and an append-only changes.ndjson — where every release is pinned by digest. That property is what makes a citation from it durable. What a citable fact looks like A fact that survives review is not a paraphrase of a homepage. It names four things: the claim itself , stated plainly; the source dataset , with its release_id and artifact_sha256 ; the as-of date of the release; a resolvable link to the dataset so any reader can re-verify. For example, from the Sourcey agent-readiness release release_id sha256:371cbf65650abf5756c967b1f1da9df607be4b1bb0c0b93aaf2dcf0a36e75d3e ( artifact_sha256:67c4edef061ca4ea60cef1e1bc246d2ce0b7d6b12e227c0811d7405d3d0a63ac , effective 2026-10-11), the registry records a per-product "agent readiness" profile for a named job — for instance that Sentry's error-event reporting interface is profiled with a pinned revision_digest and a policy version kind-2026-10-12 . The point is not the grade; it is that the grade is attached to a digest a reader can check against https://sourcey.com/agent-readiness.json . Why this matters for agents specifically Human writers get the benefit of the doubt. Agents do not, and should not. An agent that cites a digest-pinned registry is making a falsifiable claim: re-hash the file and see. That property is what lets a downstream system — another agent, a verification harness, a human reviewer — trust the fact without trusting the agent that produced it. The practical pattern is small: prefer sources that content-address their releases; record the digest and the as-of date alongside the claim; link the dataset, not a marketing page; treat a failed digest check as a dead citation, not a rounding error. The takeaway If you want an agent's output to be citable, give it sources that cannot quietly change underneath it. Digest-pinned open registries make "trust me" unnecessary: the bytes either match the citation or they do not. For agent-produced research, that is the difference between a claim and evidence. Start from a registry that pins its releases — sourcey.com is a working example — and the provenance problem shrinks to a hash comparison.
